questions.q: The conflict known in the colonies as the French and Indian War was part of a larger worldwide struggle called what?
options: The War of the Spanish Succession
The War of Jenkins' Ear
The Seven Years' War
The Thirty Years' War
questions.explain: The North American fighting was one theater of the global Seven Years' War (1756-1763) between Britain and France and their allies.

questions.q: In 1754 a young Virginia militia officer's clash with a French party in western Pennsylvania helped ignite the war. Who was he?
options: Horatio Gates
George Washington
Daniel Morgan
Nathanael Greene
questions.explain: Lieutenant Colonel George Washington's skirmish near Great Meadows and the surrender at Fort Necessity in 1754 were early events of the conflict.

questions.q: The Albany Plan of Union of 1754, which proposed a colonial council for defense and western affairs, is most closely linked to which colonial leader?
options: John Hancock
Patrick Henry
Richard Henry Lee
Benjamin Franklin
questions.explain: Franklin drafted the plan at the Albany Congress; colonial assemblies and the Crown both rejected it.

questions.q: Which agreement of 1763 ended the Seven Years' War?
options: The Treaty of Greenville
The Treaty of Paris
The Treaty of Utrecht
The Treaty of Ghent
questions.explain: The 1763 Treaty of Paris gave Britain Canada and French claims east of the Mississippi River.

questions.q: As a result of the 1763 peace settlement, which power lost nearly all of its mainland North American holdings east of the Mississippi River?
options: France
Portugal
Spain
The Netherlands
questions.explain: France ceded Canada and its lands east of the Mississippi to Britain, and handed Louisiana west of the river to Spain.

questions.q: In the settlement of 1763, what did Britain receive from Spain?
options: Cuba
Louisiana
Texas
Florida
questions.explain: Spain gave up Florida to Britain; Cuba, taken by British forces, was returned to Spain, and Louisiana had gone from France to Spain.

questions.q: Pontiac's War of 1763 began when Native nations of the Great Lakes and Ohio Country did what?
options: Joined British forces to drive Spanish settlers from Florida
Signed a treaty giving the Ohio Valley to Pennsylvania
Attacked British forts after the French withdrawal
Moved eastward to settle near Atlantic coast trading posts
questions.explain: Native leaders such as the Ottawa war leader Pontiac resisted British occupation of former French posts and rising settler pressure.

questions.q: What was the main purpose of the Proclamation of 1763?
options: To limit colonial settlement west of the Appalachians
To place new duties on sugar and molasses imports
To end the Atlantic slave trade to the colonies
To require colonists to house British soldiers at home
questions.explain: Britain tried to avoid costly frontier wars by reserving western land for Native nations and regulating land purchases.

questions.q: Many colonists, including land speculators and veterans, resented the Proclamation of 1763 mainly because it:
options: required them to pay a tax on tea
banned trade with the French West Indies
closed western lands they hoped to claim
forced them to convert to the Church of England
questions.explain: The line threatened western land claims and speculation, contributing to colonial distrust of imperial decisions made in London.

questions.q: Why did Parliament decide to raise new revenue in the colonies after 1763?
options: British merchants demanded protection from cheaper colonial manufactures
Spain had demanded repayment for supplies sent during the war
Parliament wanted to punish colonial assemblies that had defied the Crown
Britain had a large war debt and needed to pay for troops in North America
questions.explain: Victory in the Seven Years' War nearly doubled Britain's national debt, and ministers argued that colonists should help fund their own defense.

questions.q: The Sugar Act of 1764 angered many merchants chiefly because it:
options: imposed a ban on all colonial trade with the French West Indies
tightened enforcement with juryless vice-admiralty court trials
required colonial families to provide housing for British troops
placed a direct tax on every legal paper and newspaper sold
questions.explain: The act lowered the molasses duty but enforced it strictly, sending smuggling cases to juryless admiralty courts.

questions.q: The Stamp Act of 1765 required colonists to buy stamped paper for:
options: glass, lead, paint, paper, and tea imported from Britain
tea sold by the East India Company through approved agents
newspapers, legal documents, and other printed items
imported molasses, sugar, and wine from the Caribbean colonies
questions.explain: It was the first direct internal tax Parliament imposed on the colonies, falling on printed materials.

questions.q: Which slogan expressed colonial objections to the Stamp Act?
options: Give me liberty or give me death
No taxation without representation
United we stand, divided we fall
Don't tread on me
questions.explain: Colonists argued they could be taxed only by assemblies in which they were represented, not by a Parliament in which they had no elected members.

questions.q: Britain's defense of "virtual representation" claimed that colonists were represented in Parliament because:
options: members of Parliament spoke for the interests of all British subjects
colonial assemblies could veto any law passed by Parliament
the king named one delegate from each colony to sit in Parliament
colonial agents in London held voting seats in the House of Commons
questions.explain: Supporters said every member represented the whole empire; colonists answered that only elected representatives could tax them.

questions.q: The Stamp Act Congress of 1765 is significant because it:
options: created a colonial army to resist collection of the stamp tax
declared the colonies independent and named a new national leader
drafted a plan for a permanent national government
united delegates from many colonies against a parliamentary tax
questions.explain: Delegates from nine colonies met in New York and issued resolutions asserting that only their own assemblies could tax them.

questions.q: Which group, formed in port towns, used protests and intimidation of stamp distributors to resist the Stamp Act?
options: Loyalist Associators
Green Mountain Boys
Sons of Liberty
Minutemen
questions.explain: The Sons of Liberty organized crowd action and boycotts, and many stamp agents resigned before the law took effect.

questions.q: When Parliament repealed the Stamp Act in 1766, it also passed the Declaratory Act, which asserted that:
options: colonial assemblies could tax themselves without review in London
Parliament could make laws binding the colonies in all cases
colonists must be given elected seats in the House of Commons
colonial courts had the right to overrule acts of Parliament
questions.explain: The Declaratory Act kept Parliament's claim of full authority over the colonies even as the tax was withdrawn.

questions.q: The Townshend Acts of 1767 placed duties on imported goods such as:
options: glass, lead, paint, paper, and tea
wine, rum, molasses, sugar, and coffee
wool, linen, silk, cotton, and leather
iron, nails, salt, rope, and window curtains
questions.explain: These import duties were designed to raise money to pay the salaries of colonial governors and judges.

questions.q: John Dickinson's Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania argued that the Townshend duties:
options: should be resisted at once by organizing armed militia companies
should be accepted to preserve peace within the British empire
were legal because the colonies were virtually represented in Parliament
were an unconstitutional tax to raise revenue, not regulate trade
questions.explain: Dickinson accepted regulation of trade but denied Parliament's right to tax colonists for revenue, urging peaceful protest.

questions.q: During the boycotts of British goods in the 1760s and 1770s, women such as those in the Daughters of Liberty contributed by:
options: spinning homespun cloth and refusing imported items
serving as delegates to the Stamp Act Congress
commanding militia companies
writing the Massachusetts Circular Letter
questions.explain: Household production and consumption choices made nonimportation agreements effective and gave women a visible political role.

questions.q: The Massachusetts Circular Letter of 1768 urged other colonial assemblies to:
options: approve payment of the Stamp Act tax by their assemblies
send colonial troops to defend Boston against the redcoats
coordinate opposition to the Townshend duties
petition the king to appoint royal governors in each colony
questions.explain: Samuel Adams and James Otis drafted it, and British officials ordered the assembly to withdraw it, deepening the dispute.

questions.q: The Boston Massacre of March 1770 took place when:
options: colonists threw chests of tea into the harbor in protest
militia and redcoats clashed on the road to Concord
British troops burned a village outside Boston at night
British soldiers fired into a crowd, killing five colonists
questions.explain: Five Bostonians died; the event was widely publicized by patriot writers and Paul Revere's engraving.

questions.q: Which man of African and Native descent was among those killed in the Boston Massacre?
options: Prince Hall
Crispus Attucks
Salem Poor
Peter Salem
questions.explain: Attucks, a sailor, became an early symbol of the patriot cause and of Black participation in the Revolution.

questions.q: After the Boston Massacre, the British soldiers on trial were defended by:
options: John Adams
John Hancock
Samuel Adams
Paul Revere
questions.explain: John Adams defended Captain Preston and the soldiers, and most were acquitted, which he later called one of his most worthy acts.

questions.q: The Gaspee affair of 1772 involved colonists who:
options: captured Fort Ticonderoga from the British garrison
dumped chests of tea into Charleston harbor at night
seized the royal governor's mansion in Williamsburg
burned a British customs schooner off Rhode Island
questions.explain: The attack on the revenue ship HMS Gaspee led Britain to consider sending suspects to England for trial, alarming colonists.

questions.q: The Committees of Correspondence, organized beginning in 1772, were important because they:
options: drafted the first written constitutions of the new states
commanded militia units training outside Boston and Concord
shared news and coordinated resistance among towns and colonies
collected customs duties on behalf of the royal governors
questions.explain: These networks spread information quickly and prepared the way for intercolonial cooperation and the First Continental Congress.

questions.q: Which Boston leader is most closely associated with founding the Committees of Correspondence?
options: James Otis Sr.
Samuel Adams
Joseph Warren
Thomas Hutchinson
questions.explain: Samuel Adams helped launch the Boston committee in 1772 and promoted similar groups across the colonies.

questions.q: The Tea Act of 1773 allowed which company to sell tea directly to the colonies at a low price?
options: The Hudson's Bay Company
The Virginia Company
The Dutch West India Company
The East India Company
questions.explain: The act aimed to rescue the struggling East India Company; colonists saw it as a trick to make them accept Parliament's tax on tea.

questions.q: The Boston Tea Party of December 1773 was a protest in which colonists:
options: destroyed chests of tea belonging to the East India Company
attacked a British regiment stationed on Boston Common
seized the Massachusetts State House and the royal governor
burned stamped paper belonging to royal tax collectors
questions.explain: Disguised protesters dumped 342 chests of tea into Boston Harbor to prevent it from being landed and taxed.

questions.q: Britain's response to the Boston Tea Party was a set of laws the colonists called:
options: the Townshend Acts
the Intolerable Acts
the Declaratory Acts
the Navigation Acts
questions.explain: Known in Britain as the Coercive Acts, they punished Massachusetts and are often listed as a final spark toward the First Continental Congress.

questions.q: The Boston Port Act of 1774 closed Boston Harbor until:
options: colonial assemblies were dissolved
the Stamp Act was repealed
the destroyed tea was paid for
Massachusetts accepted a new governor
questions.explain: The closure was meant to isolate Boston economically; other colonies sent food and supplies in support.

questions.q: Which feature of the 1774 Massachusetts Government Act alarmed colonists in other colonies?
options: It limited town meetings and ended the elected colonial council
It opened western lands to British investors and speculators
It required every colony to feed and house British regiments
It banned the printing of colonial newspapers and pamphlets
questions.explain: The law reduced self-government in Massachusetts and made colonists elsewhere fear similar treatment.

questions.q: The Quebec Act of 1774 irritated many colonists in part because it:
options: taxed colonial exports shipped to Britain and its islands
ended all trade between Canada and the thirteen colonies
enlarged Quebec into the Ohio Valley and protected Catholicism
granted Quebec an elected assembly modeled on New England's
questions.explain: The act enlarged Quebec toward lands colonists wanted and tolerated Catholicism, which many Protestants disliked.

questions.q: The First Continental Congress met in 1774 in which city?
options: New York
Boston
Williamsburg
Philadelphia
questions.explain: Delegates from twelve colonies gathered in Philadelphia to coordinate a response to the Intolerable Acts.

questions.q: The Continental Association, adopted by the First Continental Congress, called for:
options: a declaration of independence from the Crown
a boycott of British goods, enforced by local committees
creation of a national army under a single commander
new taxes on colonial trade to fund the militia
questions.explain: Local committees monitored compliance with nonimportation, nonconsumption, and later nonexportation measures.

questions.q: Which colony was the only one of the thirteen to send no delegates to the First Continental Congress?
options: New York
Virginia
Georgia
South Carolina
questions.explain: Georgia, dependent on British protection from frontier conflict, did not attend, so twelve colonies were represented.

questions.q: The decision in the First Continental Congress to give each colony one vote was important because:
options: it ended the colonial boycott of British trade entirely
it avoided disputes over size and foreshadowed the 1787 debates
it created a second chamber based on population
it gave the largest colony a veto over congressional decisions
questions.explain: Delegates had no reliable population data and wanted unity, so each colony cast one vote, a precedent revisited in 1787.

questions.q: The first battles of the American Revolutionary War, in April 1775, took place at:
options: Saratoga and Trenton
Bunker Hill and Brooklyn
Yorktown and Camden
Lexington and Concord
questions.explain: British troops marching to seize military supplies met militia at Lexington and Concord on April 19, 1775.

questions.q: Minutemen were:
options: colonial militia members who trained to assemble on short notice
volunteers recruited by royal governors to defend loyal towns
British regulars stationed in Boston during the occupation
delegates chosen to represent colonies in Congress at Philadelphia
questions.explain: The Massachusetts minutemen were part of the militia system and responded quickly at Lexington and Concord.

questions.q: The Second Continental Congress chose which man to command the new Continental Army in June 1775?
options: Benedict Arnold
Charles Lee
Horatio Gates
George Washington
questions.explain: John Adams proposed Washington, a Virginian, in part to unite the southern colonies behind the New England-based army.

questions.q: In the summer of 1775, the Second Continental Congress sent the Olive Branch Petition to King George III in order to:
options: ask France for a military alliance against Britain
request that all colonial charters be revoked
seek reconciliation while still preparing for war
declare independence from the British Crown at once
questions.explain: Moderates led by John Dickinson hoped to avoid a break, but the king refused even to receive the petition.

questions.q: The Battle of Bunker Hill in June 1775 showed that:
options: militia could inflict heavy losses on British regulars
British forces would withdraw from Massachusetts that summer
the colonies already had an effective navy of their own
France had joined the war on the side of the Americans
questions.explain: The British won the ground but suffered more than a thousand casualties, which encouraged Americans and sobered British commanders.

questions.q: Thomas Paine's pamphlet Common Sense, published in January 1776, argued that:
options: Parliament should give the colonists seats in the Commons
the colonies should seek independence and reject monarchy
the colonies should remain loyal and trust the king
colonial assemblies should be abolished and royal rule expanded
questions.explain: Written in plain language, it sold widely and made independence a mainstream idea.

questions.q: Common Sense was effective largely because Paine:
options: wrote for ordinary readers and attacked hereditary monarchy itself
defended the king's veto while criticizing only his ministers
argued that Parliament was too weak to govern the empire
quoted extensively from Latin legal texts and classical sources
questions.explain: Paine avoided learned jargon and portrayed monarchy as unnatural, shifting blame from ministers to the king.

questions.q: Who introduced the June 1776 resolution in the Continental Congress that "these united colonies are, and of right ought to be, free and independent states"?
options: Patrick Henry
Thomas Jefferson
Richard Henry Lee
John Adams
questions.explain: Lee of Virginia moved the resolution on June 7, and Congress appointed a committee to draft a declaration while debating it.

questions.q: Which man was the principal drafter of the Declaration of Independence?
options: Roger Sherman
Benjamin Franklin
John Adams
Thomas Jefferson
questions.explain: Jefferson, aged 33, wrote the first draft for the Committee of Five and others edited it.

questions.q: The Committee of Five chosen to draft the Declaration included Jefferson, Franklin, Adams, Roger Sherman, and:
options: James Wilson of Pennsylvania
Robert R. Livingston
Patrick Henry of Virginia
John Jay of New York
questions.explain: Livingston of New York joined Sherman of Connecticut, Adams, Franklin, and Jefferson on the committee.

questions.q: On which date did the Continental Congress formally approve the final wording of the Declaration of Independence?
options: September 17, 1787
July 4, 1776
June 7, 1776
April 19, 1775
questions.explain: Congress voted for independence on July 2 and approved the Declaration's text on July 4, which is why that date is celebrated.

questions.q: Who served as president of the Second Continental Congress and was the first to sign the Declaration, in large script?
options: John Jay
Henry Laurens
John Hancock
Samuel Adams
questions.explain: Hancock's large signature became shorthand for signing one's name.

questions.q: The Declaration of Independence states that people are endowed with unalienable rights, including:
options: life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness
life, liberty, and property
trial by jury, security, and equality
freedom of speech, press, and religion
questions.explain: This famous phrase appears in the Declaration's second paragraph.

questions.q: According to the Declaration of Independence, governments derive their just powers from:
options: the consent of the governed
ancient custom and precedent
the approval of the aristocracy
divine right of kings
questions.explain: The Declaration states that when government becomes destructive of rights, the people may alter or abolish it.

questions.q: Which Enlightenment thinker most influenced the Declaration's argument that people possess natural rights and may overthrow tyrannical government?
options: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
Baron de Montesquieu
Thomas Hobbes
John Locke
questions.explain: Locke's social-contract and natural-rights ideas shaped Jefferson's reasoning; the Declaration's 'pursuit of happiness' echoes Locke's 'life, liberty, and property.'

questions.q: The Declaration of Independence is organized into a preamble, a statement of principles, a list of grievances, and:
options: a detailed plan of national government
a bill of rights listing individual liberties
a formal declaration of independence
an offer of treaty terms sent to Britain
questions.explain: After listing complaints against George III, it concludes that the united colonies are free and independent states.

questions.q: The long list of grievances in the Declaration of Independence is directed primarily at:
options: Parliament alone
King George III
the royal governors only
the East India Company
questions.explain: The document blames the king personally for abuses, reflecting colonists' view that Parliament had no authority over them.

questions.q: In his first draft, Jefferson blamed the king for the slave trade, but Congress deleted the passage. Which reason best explains the deletion?
options: Georgia and South Carolina objected, and northern merchants shared in the trade
Jefferson himself asked Congress to remove the passage before the vote
The king had already ended the slave trade in the colonies in 1775
Congress feared the passage would anger the French court and block an alliance
questions.explain: The deletion shows how slavery complicated the Declaration's claims about equality and natural rights.

questions.q: A historian arguing that the Declaration's statement "all men are created equal" contained a contradiction at the time would most likely point to:
options: the high taxes on tea
the king's control of the colonial courts
the absence of a national army
the existence of slavery in the new states
questions.explain: Many signers enslaved people, a tension that later abolitionists and reformers used to challenge the nation to live up to its stated ideals.

questions.q: Jefferson later called the Declaration "an expression of the American mind." This suggests he intended it to:
options: defend the Church of England against dissenters
state shared ideas rather than invent new ones
appeal to the monarchs of France and Spain
draft a new constitution for the thirteen states
questions.explain: Jefferson said he did not seek originality but to place common sense of the subject before the world.

questions.q: Which document, adopted in June 1776 and largely written by George Mason, influenced Jefferson's Declaration?
options: The Mayflower Compact of 1620
The Fundamental Orders of Connecticut
The Virginia Declaration of Rights
The Albany Plan of Union of 1754
questions.explain: Mason's declaration said all men are by nature equally free and independent and had natural rights, language echoed in 1776.

questions.q: John Trumbull's painting of the presentation of the Declaration of Independence hangs in:
options: the White House East Room
the Supreme Court chamber
the Library of Congress Reading Room
the Capitol Rotunda
questions.explain: Trumbull's Declaration of Independence is one of four of his large Revolutionary War paintings in the Rotunda.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the four John Trumbull paintings in the Capitol Rotunda?
options: Washington Crossing the Delaware at Trenton
General George Washington Resigning His Commission
Landing of Columbus on the Island of Guanahani
Embarkation of the Pilgrims at Delft Haven
questions.explain: Trumbull painted four scenes for the Rotunda: the Declaration, the surrenders at Saratoga and Yorktown, and Washington's resignation.

questions.q: John Trumbull's Declaration of Independence painting in the Capitol Rotunda is often mistaken for a scene of the signing. What does it actually show?
options: The Committee of Five presenting its draft to Congress on June 28, 1776
Delegates signing the engrossed parchment on August 2, 1776
Congress voting for the Lee Resolution on July 2, 1776
Washington accepting command of the Continental Army in 1775
questions.explain: It shows the Committee of Five presenting the draft; delegates mostly signed the engrossed copy later, on August 2, 1776. Trumbull also painted figures who were not all in the room.

questions.q: The engrossed (parchment) copy of the Declaration was signed mainly on what date?
options: August 2, 1776
July 4, 1776
June 7, 1776
October 1, 1777
questions.explain: Most delegates signed the engrossed copy on August 2 after Congress ordered it prepared.

questions.q: How many delegates are traditionally counted as signers of the Declaration of Independence?
questions.explain: Fifty-six delegates from the thirteen states signed the Declaration.

questions.q: The oldest signer of the Declaration of Independence was:
options: Benjamin Franklin
Samuel Adams
John Hancock
John Witherspoon
questions.explain: Benjamin Franklin, born in 1706, was 70 years old in 1776, making him the oldest signer of the Declaration of Independence.

questions.q: Which signer of the Declaration of Independence was a Catholic planter and the only Catholic to sign?
options: William Paca of Maryland
Thomas Stone of Maryland
Charles Carroll of Carrollton
Richard Stockton of New Jersey
questions.explain: Carroll of Maryland was the only Catholic signer and the last surviving signer; he died in 1832.

questions.q: Which signer of the Declaration of Independence also served as president of the College of New Jersey (Princeton) and was a Presbyterian minister?
options: Benjamin Rush
John Witherspoon
George Wythe
Lyman Hall
questions.explain: Witherspoon, a Scottish-born clergyman and educator, was the only active minister to sign.

questions.q: Which two founders, both former presidents and both members of the committee that drafted the Declaration, died on July 4, 1826?
options: Thomas Jefferson and John Adams
Thomas Jefferson and James Monroe
George Washington and James Madison
John Adams and Benjamin Franklin
questions.explain: Jefferson and Adams died on the fiftieth anniversary of the Declaration.

questions.q: Jefferson wrote his own epitaph, which did not mention his presidency but did list:
options: the Embargo Act of 1807
the Louisiana Purchase of 1803
the Monroe Doctrine of 1823
the Declaration of Independence
questions.explain: His chosen epitaph named authorship of the Declaration and the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom and founding the University of Virginia.

questions.q: When Congress issued the Declaration of Independence, what practical aim did it serve in international politics?
options: It created a national tax system for the new states
It helped justify seeking foreign aid and alliances
It formed a national bank to fund the army
It ended the Intolerable Acts imposed on Boston
questions.explain: Independence made it easier to seek recognition and military help, especially from France.

questions.q: Colonists who remained loyal to Britain during the Revolution were called:
options: Federalists
Whigs
Loyalists
Patriots
questions.explain: Loyalists, also called Tories, are often estimated at 15 to 20 percent of the white population, with numbers varying widely by region.

questions.q: Which group of enslaved people did Lord Dunmore's 1775 proclamation offer freedom to?
options: Those who had earlier purchased their own freedom
All enslaved people held anywhere in the colony of Virginia
Those who had already served in the Continental Army
Those enslaved by rebels who joined the British forces
questions.explain: Dunmore, Virginia's royal governor, promised freedom to enslaved men owned by patriots who joined the British, which pushed some Virginians toward independence.

questions.q: Which general crossed the Delaware River on Christmas night 1776 and surprised Hessian troops at Trenton?
options: Nathanael Greene
Charles Cornwallis
George Washington
Benedict Arnold
questions.explain: The victory at Trenton boosted morale after a string of defeats around New York.

questions.q: In the summer and fall of 1776, the Continental Army suffered a series of defeats in which area?
options: New York
Virginia
South Carolina
Georgia
questions.explain: Washington lost the battles around New York City and retreated through New Jersey before the successes at Trenton and Princeton.

questions.q: Which battle in 1777 is often seen as the turning point of the war because it convinced France to enter the conflict?
options: Bunker Hill
Saratoga
Camden
Trenton
questions.explain: General Burgoyne's surrender at Saratoga in October 1777 persuaded France to ally with the Americans.

questions.q: Which American diplomat, already famous in France, led the commissioners who signed the 1778 treaties of alliance and commerce with France?
options: John Adams
John Jay
Henry Laurens
Benjamin Franklin
questions.explain: Franklin's popularity in France and persistence helped bring about the treaty with Louis XVI's government.

questions.q: The winter of 1777-1778 at Valley Forge is remembered for:
options: a decisive victory over General Howe's army in open battle
hardship in camp and improved army discipline
a mutiny by Hessian troops serving the American cause
the surrender of Philadelphia to Washington's forces
questions.explain: Despite shortages and disease, drilling led by Baron von Steuben made the Continental Army more effective.

questions.q: Which Prussian officer drilled the Continental Army at Valley Forge?
options: Marquis de Lafayette
Thaddeus Kosciuszko
Friedrich von Steuben
Comte de Rochambeau
questions.explain: Steuben introduced standardized drills and a training manual that became the basis for army instruction.

questions.q: Who was the Marquis de Lafayette in the American Revolution?
options: a French aristocrat who became a trusted aide to Washington
a Spanish naval commander who aided the French blockade
a Dutch banker who loaned money to Congress
a Hessian commander who changed sides in 1777
questions.explain: Lafayette joined Washington's staff at 19 and later helped trap Cornwallis in Virginia.

questions.q: The final major battle of the Revolutionary War, in October 1781, ended with the surrender of Lord Cornwallis at:
options: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
Charleston, South Carolina
Saratoga, New York
Yorktown, Virginia
questions.explain: French and American forces, supported by a French fleet, trapped Cornwallis on the Yorktown peninsula.

questions.q: The victory at Yorktown depended heavily on:
options: the earlier capture of New York City by Washington
a British retreat to Canada before the siege began
French sea power off Virginia and allied teamwork
Spanish troops from Louisiana arriving in Virginia
questions.explain: The French fleet under de Grasse blocked British relief, while Rochambeau's and Washington's troops besieged the town.

questions.q: Which treaty formally ended the American Revolutionary War in 1783?
options: Jay's Treaty
The Treaty of Paris
The Treaty of Utrecht
The Treaty of Ghent
questions.explain: Britain recognized American independence and set boundaries stretching west to the Mississippi River.

questions.q: Under the Treaty of Paris of 1783, the western boundary of the United States was set at:
options: the Rocky Mountains
the Mississippi River
the Ohio River
the Appalachian Mountains
questions.explain: The treaty gave the new nation land west to the Mississippi, north to the Great Lakes region, and south to Florida's northern border.

questions.q: Which two American negotiators, along with Franklin, helped secure the 1783 peace treaty?
options: Henry Laurens and Gouverneur Morris
Alexander Hamilton and Robert Morris
Thomas Jefferson and James Madison
John Jay and John Adams
questions.explain: Jay and Adams joined Franklin in negotiating terms, partly ignoring French wishes to secure favorable boundaries.

questions.q: The Treaty of Paris (1783) urged that Congress "earnestly recommend" to the states that they:
options: disband the state militias after peace
abolish the slave trade within five years
restore confiscated Loyalist property
invite the former colonies to rejoin the empire
questions.explain: The recommendation was largely ignored by state governments, and Loyalist claims remained a point of friction.

questions.q: In the Treaty of Paris of 1783, Native nations that had fought alongside Britain were:
options: left out while the treaty gave the U.S. their lands
guaranteed their independent territory by Britain
included as signers alongside the American envoys
given protection by a French alliance after the war
questions.explain: Britain gave up claims to lands where many Native nations lived without consulting them, which led to continued conflict.

questions.q: During the Revolution, most Iroquois (Haudenosaunee) nations:
options: split, with the Mohawk and others siding with Britain
moved to Canada before the fighting began in 1775
remained entirely neutral throughout the whole war
united to support the Continental Army as one confederacy
questions.explain: The Six Nations Confederacy divided: most fought for the British, while the Oneida and Tuscarora largely supported the Americans.

questions.q: In 1779 the Sullivan Expedition sent by Washington:
options: retook the city of Charleston from the British garrison
captured British forts along the St. Lawrence River in Canada
crossed the Appalachians to defend Kentucky settlements
destroyed many Haudenosaunee towns and crops in western New York
questions.explain: Washington ordered the campaign to end raids on frontier settlements, and it caused severe damage to Haudenosaunee communities.

questions.q: How did many Black Americans, both free and enslaved, take part in the Revolution?
options: They were exempt from the war
They were barred from all military service by law
They served on both sides, often hoping for freedom
They served only as diplomats
questions.explain: Thousands served the patriot cause and thousands joined the British, often motivated by promises or hopes of freedom.

questions.q: In the Continental Army, Washington at first barred Black enlistment but later reversed course mainly because:
options: France made integration of the army a condition of its alliance
the army needed soldiers and the British offered freedom
Congress had abolished slavery in the states by a law in 1777
the Declaration of Independence required Black men to be enlisted
questions.explain: Manpower shortages and Dunmore's proclamation pushed Washington to accept free Black enlistments and eventually enslaved substitutes in some states.

questions.q: The First Rhode Island Regiment of 1778 was notable because:
options: it consisted entirely of Hessian deserters from British lines
it was composed mainly of Black and Native soldiers, many once enslaved
it served only as the crew of a privateer sailing from Newport
it was the first American unit to cross the Delaware River in 1776
questions.explain: Rhode Island promised freedom to enslaved men who enlisted, and the regiment fought at the Battle of Rhode Island.

questions.q: Phillis Wheatley, a formerly enslaved woman in Boston, is remembered as:
options: the author who wrote the first draft of the Declaration
a spy who carried secret messages to the Continental Army
the first African American to publish a book of poetry
a leader of the crowd at the Boston Massacre in 1770
questions.explain: Her 1773 poems helped challenge ideas that African people were intellectually inferior, and she also wrote about liberty and George Washington.

questions.q: Who was a Black Patriot of Massachusetts who fought at Bunker Hill and was commended by American officers?
options: Peter Poyas
Richard Allen
Absalom Jones
Salem Poor
questions.explain: Poor was recognized in a petition from officers for his bravery at Bunker Hill.

questions.q: Women contributed to the Revolutionary War effort by:
options: running farms and shops and following the army
voting in elections in nearly every one of the new states
commanding regiments in the field during major campaigns
serving as elected delegates in the Continental Congress
questions.explain: Camp followers, nurses, and women managing farms and shops were essential, and a few disguised themselves to fight.

questions.q: Abigail Adams' 1776 letter urging her husband to "remember the ladies" asked him to:
options: give women legal protections in the new laws
grant women full voting rights at once
free the enslaved people held in Massachusetts
end the Intolerable Acts in Massachusetts
questions.explain: She warned of rebellion if women's interests were ignored, but did not demand a vote; the letter is an early statement of women's legal concerns.

questions.q: How did Mercy Otis Warren contribute to the Revolutionary cause?
options: a general who commanded a Massachusetts regiment at Bunker Hill
a playwright and historian who wrote satire and a history of the war
a diplomat who represented Congress at the court of France
a merchant who funded the Continental Army from her shipping profits
questions.explain: Warren's plays attacked royal officials and she wrote History of the Rise, Progress and Termination of the American Revolution.

questions.q: A woman called "Molly Pitcher" in legend is said to have:
options: served as a spy for the army in British-held New York
written the first draft of the Declaration of Independence
carried water and helped man a cannon at the Battle of Monmouth
crossed the Delaware River with Washington in December 1776
questions.explain: The story is often linked to Mary Ludwig Hays at Monmouth in 1778, though details are debated by historians.

questions.q: The Battle of Yorktown ended active large-scale fighting, but the peace treaty was signed in:
questions.explain: Fighting largely ended after Yorktown in 1781, and negotiators signed the Treaty of Paris in 1783.

questions.q: In 1783, officers of the Continental Army angry about unpaid wages circulated the Newburgh Conspiracy, but Washington:
options: ordered the ringleaders arrested and tried by court-martial
resigned his command in protest and left for Mount Vernon
led the officers in a march on Congress in Philadelphia
urged them to trust Congress, easing a threat to civilian rule
questions.explain: Washington's emotional address at Newburgh helped end the crisis and reinforced the principle of civilian control of the military.

questions.q: In December 1783 George Washington gave a powerful example of civilian control of the military when he:
options: refused to retire from command
accepted a crown offered by his officers
resigned his commission to Congress
marched his army to Philadelphia
questions.explain: Washington resigned in Annapolis, Maryland, and returned to Mount Vernon, an act admired across Europe.

questions.q: Why did many Americans in the 1780s distrust the idea of a permanent standing army in peacetime?
options: They believed a peacetime army would be too small to matter
They feared it could threaten liberty and civilian government
They wanted every defense duty left to the French navy
They thought only Britain could afford to pay for one
questions.explain: Many leaders saw standing armies as tools of tyranny and preferred state militias, a worry reflected in constitutional debates.

questions.q: The Constitution gave Congress the power to raise armies but limited army appropriations to how long?
options: Two years
One month
Ten years
Five years
questions.explain: The two-year limit lets the House, elected every two years, review army funding regularly.

questions.q: Which complaint about British troops appears among the grievances in the Declaration of Independence?
options: Keeping standing armies in peacetime without consent
Forcing colonists to enlist in the royal navy for life
Banning the militia from training on town commons
Burning coastal towns before the first shots of the war
questions.explain: The Declaration charged the king with keeping standing armies and quartering troops, grievances later reflected in the Third Amendment.

questions.q: Many state constitutions written in 1776-1780 shared which feature?
options: An established national church supported by all states
A hereditary governor chosen from leading families
A written plan limiting power and often listing rights
A single national legislature with absolute powers
questions.explain: States made written constitutions the foundation of republican government, with explicit protections for rights.

questions.q: The Massachusetts Constitution of 1780 is notable because it:
options: abolished the legislature in favor of a council
was drafted by a special convention and approved by voters
was written by one governor and accepted without a vote
was imposed on the state by the Continental Congress
questions.explain: John Adams wrote most of it, and the ratification process by voters became a model for later constitution making.

questions.q: In the 1780s, a Massachusetts court cited the state constitution's statement that "all men are born free and equal" in the case of:
options: Marbury v. Madison, a ruling on judicial review of statutes
Prigg v. Pennsylvania, a ruling on fugitive slave laws
Dred Scott v. Sandford, a ruling on slavery and citizenship
Quock Walker, which helped bring an end to slavery in Massachusetts
questions.explain: Massachusetts court rulings in the early 1780s, in the Quock Walker cases, held slavery incompatible with the state constitution, and slavery faded there.

questions.q: Which northern state passed the first gradual emancipation law in 1780?
options: Pennsylvania
Massachusetts
New Jersey
New York
questions.explain: Pennsylvania's Gradual Abolition Act of 1780 freed children born to enslaved mothers after the act once they had served until age 28, a model for other northern states.

questions.q: Gradual emancipation laws in northern states generally:
options: compensated owners with western land for each person freed
ended slavery in every state, North and South, by 1800
freed every enslaved person in the state on the same day
freed children of the enslaved at a set age, not adults
questions.explain: These laws slowly reduced slavery in the North, though many people remained enslaved for years.

questions.q: Vermont's 1777 constitution was notable because it:
options: created a monarchy
banned adult slavery
required a state church
gave women the vote
questions.explain: Vermont, which was not yet a state, prohibited adult slavery in its constitution, though enforcement was uneven.

questions.q: Which religious group in Pennsylvania took early antislavery positions and helped found the first abolition society?
options: Congregationalists
Baptists
Quakers
Anglicans
questions.explain: Quakers helped form the Society for the Relief of Free Negroes Unlawfully Held in Bondage in Philadelphia in 1775, later the Pennsylvania Abolition Society.

questions.q: New Jersey's 1776 constitution briefly allowed some women to vote because it:
options: contained a special clause granting women the right to vote
used "inhabitants" with property and never mentioned sex
was drafted by a committee that included women delegates
abolished property requirements for every free voter
questions.explain: Property-holding women, including some single women, voted in New Jersey until an 1807 law limited suffrage to white men.

questions.q: Under many state constitutions after 1776, the right to vote was:
options: limited mainly to adult men who owned property
granted to women and men equally
granted to all adults
limited to Protestants only in every state
questions.explain: Property qualifications were common, though they varied, and some states allowed free Black men to vote at first.

questions.q: The Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, drafted by Jefferson and passed in 1786, declared that:
options: the Anglican Church was the official church of Virginia
only Christians could hold public office in the state
religion could not be taught or mentioned in public schools
no person could be compelled to support or attend any religion
questions.explain: Madison guided it through the Virginia legislature, and it ended state financial support for churches in Virginia.

questions.q: Which document by Jefferson is carved on a wall inside the Jefferson Memorial?
options: The Emancipation Proclamation and the Gettysburg Address
Washington's Farewell Address and Adams's inaugural speech
Excerpts from the Declaration and the Statute for Religious Freedom
The Louisiana Purchase Treaty and the Lewis and Clark journals
questions.explain: The memorial's panels quote his Declaration, his religious freedom statute, and other writings.

questions.q: The Jefferson Memorial quotation "I have sworn upon the altar of God eternal hostility against every form of tyranny over the mind of man" expressed Jefferson's:
options: opposition to the proposed Constitution of 1787
support for freedom of thought and religion
defense of the king's authority over the colonies
wish to abolish Parliament and the House of Lords
questions.explain: Jefferson wrote it in a letter to Benjamin Rush in 1800 amid political attacks on his religious views.

questions.q: The first national constitution of the United States, ratified in 1781, was called the:
options: Articles of Confederation
Albany Plan of Union
Virginia Plan of Government
Declaration of Rights and Grievances
questions.explain: The Articles created a loose league of states with a one-chamber Congress and no separate executive or national court system.

questions.q: The Articles of Confederation took effect only after which state finally agreed to ratify in 1781, once western land claims were addressed?
options: Virginia
New York
Maryland
Georgia
questions.explain: Maryland held out until states with large western claims, notably Virginia, agreed to cede them to the national government.

questions.q: Under the Articles of Confederation, how did the Congress vote on most measures?
options: Each member had one vote, and the president could break ties
Each state had two votes, with unanimity needed for all laws
Each state's vote was based on its population, with a simple majority
Each state had one vote, and important laws needed nine states
questions.explain: The equal state vote and the nine-state supermajority made it hard to act, a flaw the 1787 convention tried to fix.

questions.q: One major weakness of the national government under the Articles of Confederation was that it:
options: controlled all trade among the states and with Europe
allowed national courts to overturn state laws freely
had a powerful president who could veto every bill passed
could not levy taxes and had to request money from the states
questions.explain: Congress could only ask states for funds, and many refused or paid late, leaving the government short of revenue.

questions.q: Amending the Articles of Confederation required approval by:
options: all thirteen state legislatures
three-fourths of the states
two-thirds of the states
a majority of Congress alone
questions.explain: The unanimity rule meant a single state could block reform, as Rhode Island did with an impost plan in 1781.

questions.q: Which proposal, blocked when one state refused to agree, would have given Congress a small tariff on imports in the 1780s?
options: The excise
The impost
The bounty
The embargo
questions.explain: Rhode Island rejected the 1781 impost, then New York blocked a revised version, showing the limits of unanimity.

questions.q: The Land Ordinance of 1785 provided for the survey of western lands into:
options: plantations along the Ohio River and its tributaries
square plots of ten acres sold only to veterans
townships divided into 36 sections
large estates granted to army officers
questions.explain: The grid system organized the Northwest Territory for sale and reserved a section in each township to support public schools.

questions.q: The Land Ordinance of 1785 set aside the sixteenth section of each township for:
options: Native American reserves
the support of public schools
veterans of the war
religious missions
questions.explain: This provision reflected the belief that education was necessary for republican citizens.

questions.q: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 created a process for:
options: organizing western territories and admitting them as new states
dividing the original thirteen states into smaller districts
removing Native nations from all lands north of the Ohio River
taxing western settlers to repay the Revolutionary war debt
questions.explain: The law promised that territories would become states on equal terms once they reached a population threshold.

questions.q: Which provision of the Northwest Ordinance was a significant step in early restrictions on slavery?
options: It required enslaved people in Virginia to be freed at once
It banned slavery in every territory of the United States
It guaranteed settlers the right to own enslaved people
It prohibited slavery in the territory north of the Ohio River
questions.explain: The ban applied to the Northwest Territory, though fugitive slave provisions and illegal practices existed there.

questions.q: The Northwest Ordinance included which protections for settlers that foreshadowed the Bill of Rights?
options: A guarantee of the right to keep and bear arms
A national bank, tariff rights, and federal roads
Religious freedom, jury trials, and schools
A ban on all taxes and a guarantee of free land
questions.explain: The ordinance stated that religion, morality, and knowledge were necessary to good government and listed several civil liberties.

questions.q: Native nations in the Ohio Country responded to the Northwest Ordinance by:
options: resisting settlement by forming a defensive confederacy
welcoming settlers as neighbors and selling them farmland
signing a defensive alliance with Spain against Britain
selling all of their land to Congress in a single treaty
questions.explain: Despite promises of fair treatment, settlement led to war, including the defeat of American forces in 1791 before Wayne's victory in 1794.

questions.q: A key diplomatic problem for the Confederation government in the 1780s was that:
options: France demanded immediate repayment of every wartime loan
Britain had closed every American port to foreign trade by law
Spain had invaded Georgia and seized several forts
Britain kept Northwest forts and states ignored treaty duties
questions.explain: Britain delayed leaving posts such as Detroit, citing unpaid prewar debts and Loyalist claims that states had not honored.

questions.q: Spain's closing of the lower Mississippi River to American shipping in 1784 hurt which group most?
options: New England whalers sailing out of Nantucket
Pennsylvania ironmakers selling to eastern cities
Western farmers who shipped goods down the river
Southern tobacco planters near the Atlantic coast
questions.explain: Westerners relied on New Orleans to export crops, and the dispute revealed Congress's weakness in foreign policy.

questions.q: Shays' Rebellion of 1786-1787 was an uprising by:
options: Virginia tobacco planters facing falling prices
debt-burdened farmers in western Massachusetts
Pennsylvania farmers who distilled whiskey for sale
New York dockworkers demanding higher wages
questions.explain: Farmers facing foreclosures and high taxes closed courts and attacked a federal arsenal in Springfield.

questions.q: Shays' Rebellion convinced many leaders that:
options: the British should be asked to resume their rule over the states
the state governments ought to be abolished entirely
the Articles of Confederation were strong enough as written
the national government needed more power to maintain order
questions.explain: The uprising alarmed political elites and encouraged support for calling a convention in Philadelphia.

questions.q: Which Revolutionary War veteran led the Massachusetts farmers in the 1786 uprising?
options: Henry Knox
Nathanael Greene
Daniel Shays
Ethan Allen
questions.explain: Shays, a former captain in the Continental Army, became the figurehead of the movement.

questions.q: In Shays' Rebellion, why was the Confederation Congress unable to raise a national army quickly?
options: It lacked money and the power to compel states
It had no soldiers to spare because all were in Ohio
It sympathized with the farmers and refused to act
It had been dissolved by vote of the state legislatures
questions.explain: Massachusetts relied on privately funded militia, which showed the limits of Congress's authority.

questions.q: The Annapolis Convention of 1786, attended by only five states, ended by:
options: drafting a new declaration of rights for the thirteen states
calling for a wider meeting at Philadelphia in 1787
creating a national army to put down Shays's followers
admitting Vermont as the fourteenth state of the union
questions.explain: Hamilton drafted the report urging all states to meet in Philadelphia the next year.

questions.q: The Constitutional Convention of 1787 met in which city?
options: Philadelphia
Annapolis
Boston
New York
questions.explain: Delegates met in the Pennsylvania State House, now called Independence Hall.

questions.q: Who presided over the Constitutional Convention?
options: Benjamin Franklin
Alexander Hamilton
George Washington
James Madison
questions.explain: Washington's reputation lent legitimacy to the secret deliberations.

questions.q: Which delegate is often called the "Father of the Constitution" for his planning and notes at the convention?
options: James Wilson
James Madison
Roger Sherman
Gouverneur Morris
questions.explain: Madison prepared the Virginia Plan and kept the most complete record of the debates.

questions.q: The convention was originally called to:
options: create a monarchy to unite the states
declare independence from the British Crown
write a new bill of rights for the nation
revise the Articles of Confederation
questions.explain: Congress authorized a meeting to amend the Articles, but delegates chose to write an entirely new framework.

questions.q: The delegates at the Philadelphia convention agreed to keep their debates secret mainly so that:
options: British spies would not learn of the delegates' plan
state legislatures would not be able to vote on it
newspapers had been banned from the city of Philadelphia
members could speak freely and change their positions
questions.explain: Secrecy let delegates speak freely, test ideas and change their minds without public pressure, which made compromise easier. Madison's notes of the debates were not published until 1840.

questions.q: Which state refused to send any delegates to the Constitutional Convention?
options: New Hampshire
Rhode Island
Georgia
Delaware
questions.explain: Rhode Island, fearing a stronger central government, stayed away; the other twelve states were represented.

questions.q: The Virginia Plan proposed a national legislature in which representation would be based on:
options: population or wealth
property ownership alone
appointment by governors
equal votes for each state
questions.explain: Larger states favored this approach because it gave them greater influence.

questions.q: The New Jersey Plan, introduced by William Paterson, proposed:
options: a strong executive with absolute veto over every state law
a Congress elected directly by voters in each new district
a one-house legislature with equal representation for each state
a two-house legislature with seats apportioned by population
questions.explain: Smaller states wanted to keep the equal vote they had under the Articles, while strengthening Congress's powers.

questions.q: The Great Compromise (Connecticut Compromise) settled the dispute between large and small states by creating:
options: a single house elected by population with no second chamber
a council appointed by the president to represent each state
a House by population and a Senate with equal state votes
two houses, both apportioned by the population of states
questions.explain: Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth helped craft the plan that combined elements of both proposals.

questions.q: Which Connecticut delegate is most closely linked with proposing the compromise on representation?
options: Roger Sherman
William Paterson
Edmund Randolph
Rufus King
questions.explain: Sherman, also a signer of the Declaration and Articles, urged a bicameral legislature with different bases of representation.

questions.q: Under the Great Compromise, revenue bills must begin in the:
options: The Electoral College of electors
House of Representatives
The Supreme Court acting alone
The Senate of the United States
questions.explain: The House, as the body closest to the people, was given the power to start tax bills.

questions.q: How many senators does each state have?
options: Three
Four
One
Two
questions.explain: Equal representation in the Senate reflects the compromise that gave small states equal footing.

questions.q: The Three-Fifths Compromise counted each enslaved person as three-fifths of a person for purposes of:
options: the right to own land in the western territories
voting rights in presidential elections nationwide
representation in the House and direct taxation
citizenship rights under the federal Constitution
questions.explain: The formula increased the political power of slaveholding states in the House and in the Electoral College.

questions.q: Which argument did southern delegates make at the convention that led to the Three-Fifths Compromise?
options: Enslaved people should count for representation but not for taxation
Enslaved people should be freed before the Constitution took effect
Enslaved people should be allowed to vote for their representatives
Slavery should be abolished throughout the country by the year 1800
questions.explain: Northerners objected to counting people as property for representation, and the three-fifths ratio had earlier been proposed under the Articles.

questions.q: The Constitution allowed Congress to ban the importation of enslaved people after what year?
questions.explain: A compromise prevented Congress from outlawing the international slave trade for twenty years.

questions.q: Which clause of the Constitution required the return of people who escaped from slavery to another state?
options: The Contract Clause
The Elastic Clause
The Supremacy Clause
The Fugitive Slave Clause
questions.explain: Article IV required that enslaved people who escaped be returned to their owners, though the word "slave" did not appear.

questions.q: The delegates avoided using the word "slave" in the Constitution, which suggests that they:
options: were uneasy about naming slavery in a charter of liberty
wanted to hide its existence from the British government
believed that slavery was already illegal in every state
wished to end slavery immediately through the Constitution
questions.explain: Euphemisms like "other persons" show tension between the founding ideals and compromises protecting slavery.

questions.q: The Commerce Compromise at the convention allowed Congress to regulate trade and tax imports but:
options: not tax imports
not tax exports
not raise any taxes
not regulate interstate trade
questions.explain: Southern states, which depended on exporting crops, wanted protection from export taxes.

questions.q: The Electoral College was a compromise between election of the president by:
options: the Supreme Court and the Senate
the previous president and Congress
state governors and the House
Congress and election by popular vote
questions.explain: Delegates created electors chosen as each state legislature directed, balancing small states, large states, and fears of direct democracy.

questions.q: The Constitution's description of the president's election requires a candidate to win a majority of:
options: popular votes
House members
electoral votes
state legislatures
questions.explain: If no candidate has a majority, the House chooses among the top candidates, with each state delegation having one vote.

questions.q: The Constitution divides the national government into which three branches?
options: Congress, the cabinet, and the courts
Federal, state, and local governments
Legislative, executive, and judicial
House, Senate, and presidency alone
questions.explain: Separating powers was meant to prevent any person or group from holding too much authority.

questions.q: The president's power to veto legislation is best described as:
options: a limit on state power under federalism
a check by the executive on the legislature
an exercise of popular sovereignty
a check by the courts on the president
questions.explain: Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in each house.

questions.q: Which action is Congress's check on the president?
options: Impeaching and removing a president
Issuing pardons to convicted officials
Appointing judges to the federal courts
Vetoing treaties negotiated by the Senate
questions.explain: The House can impeach and the Senate tries the case, with a two-thirds vote needed to convict.

questions.q: Which branch's role is to approve or reject presidential nominees for the Supreme Court?
options: The Cabinet
The Electoral College
The Senate
The House
questions.explain: The Senate's advice and consent power checks the president's choices for judges and executive officers.

questions.q: The Constitution gives the Senate the power to:
options: impeach federal officials by majority vote
originate all bills that raise revenue
choose the president when electors disagree
ratify treaties by a two-thirds vote
questions.explain: This shared treaty power gives the executive and the Senate roles in foreign policy.

questions.q: Who has the sole power to impeach federal officials?
options: The House of Representatives
The Senate acting by a two-thirds vote
The Supreme Court on a request from Congress
The president on the advice of the cabinet
questions.explain: The House brings charges, similar to an indictment, and the Senate holds the trial.

questions.q: Which official serves as president of the Senate and votes only to break ties?
options: The Speaker
The vice president
The Senate majority leader
The chief justice
questions.explain: The Constitution gives the vice president this role, which links the executive to the legislature.

questions.q: What minimum age is required to serve in the House of Representatives?
questions.explain: The Constitution sets 25 for representatives, 30 for senators, and 35 for the president.

questions.q: How long is the term of a United States senator?
options: Six years
Two years
Four years
Eight years
questions.explain: Staggered terms mean one-third of the Senate is elected every two years.

questions.q: How often are members of the House elected?
options: Every six years
Every year
Every two years
Every four years
questions.explain: Short terms were meant to keep the House responsive to the people.

questions.q: Originally, senators were chosen by:
options: the House
the president
popular vote
state legislatures
questions.explain: The Seventeenth Amendment, ratified in 1913, established direct election.

questions.q: Which house of Congress was designed to be elected directly by voters in 1787?
options: The House of Representatives
The Electoral College of electors
The Supreme Court of the United States
The Senate of the United States
questions.explain: The framers wanted at least one body of the national legislature directly accountable to the people.

questions.q: The "necessary and proper" clause, sometimes called the elastic clause, lets Congress:
options: control the conduct of elections held in every state
override state constitutions that conflict with its laws
remove federal judges who disagree with its policies
make laws needed to carry out its listed powers
questions.explain: It has been used to justify implied powers, such as creating a national bank.

questions.q: The Supremacy Clause states that:
options: state laws outrank federal law in matters of local concern
the president controls the governments of the states
the Constitution and federal laws outrank state laws
state courts hold final authority over federal courts
questions.explain: It makes the Constitution and treaties made under it the supreme law of the land.

questions.q: Federalism refers to a system in which:
options: the president rules by decree over a national legislature
power is shared between a national government and the states
states have no authority apart from the national government
all power is held by a single monarch and his council
questions.explain: The Constitution divides authority between the national and state governments.

questions.q: Article V of the Constitution allows amendments to be proposed by:
options: a majority of Congress
a majority of the Supreme Court
the president alone
two-thirds of both houses of Congress
questions.explain: Amendments must then be ratified by three-fourths of the states, a difficult process by design.

questions.q: Why did the framers make the amendment process more flexible than the process under the Articles of Confederation?
options: they wanted the president to amend it by proclamation
they wanted a government that could adapt without unanimity
they wanted Congress to rewrite it whenever it chose
they feared the states would be left too weak to resist
questions.explain: Requiring three-fourths of states rather than all thirteen made change possible but still hard.

questions.q: Which delegate is credited with the final wording of the Preamble beginning "We the People"?
options: Edmund Randolph
James Madison
Gouverneur Morris
George Mason
questions.explain: Morris was the chief stylist of the Committee of Style, which produced the final text.

questions.q: The words "We the People" at the start of the Constitution suggest that:
options: government's authority comes from the people, not the states
the states are the source of all political authority
the president rules the nation on behalf of the people
Britain had given its approval to the new framework
questions.explain: The Preamble emphasizes popular sovereignty, a shift from the Articles' "We the undersigned delegates."

questions.q: Three delegates present at the end of the convention who refused to sign the Constitution included:
options: George Mason, Edmund Randolph, and Elbridge Gerry
James Wilson, Roger Sherman, and Rufus King
Alexander Hamilton, John Jay, and Robert Morris
Benjamin Franklin, Gouverneur Morris, and George Read
questions.explain: Mason objected to the lack of a bill of rights and Gerry feared too much national power, among other concerns.

questions.q: The Constitution was signed on September 17, 1787, by how many delegates?
options: Twenty-five
Thirteen
Thirty-nine
Fifty-five
questions.explain: Thirty-nine delegates signed, with fifty-five delegates having participated at various times.

questions.q: Benjamin Franklin's closing remark about the "rising sun" on Washington's chair at the convention expressed his hope that:
options: the convention would adjourn
the weather would clear
Washington would be king
the new government would succeed
questions.explain: Franklin said he had wondered whether the sun was rising or setting and concluded it was rising for the new nation.

questions.q: The Constitution would take effect after ratification by:
options: all thirteen of the states
nine of the thirteen states
the Confederation Congress alone
seven of the thirteen states
questions.explain: The framers deliberately avoided unanimity by requiring only nine states.

questions.q: Special state conventions, not legislatures, were chosen to ratify the Constitution mainly because:
options: Britain required that all new constitutions use conventions
the state legislatures had all been dissolved by Congress
supporters wanted approval to come directly from the people
Congress forbade state legislatures from voting on it
questions.explain: Using conventions bypassed legislators who might lose power and grounded the document in popular consent.

questions.q: Supporters of ratifying the Constitution called themselves:
options: Federalists
Republicans
Loyalists
Antifederalists
questions.explain: Federalists argued that a stronger national government was needed to protect liberty and order.

questions.q: The main objection of Antifederalists to the new Constitution was that it:
options: created a king-like office with a lifetime term of service
concentrated power in a distant government with no bill of rights
weakened the states less than the Articles of Confederation
ended all taxes and left the government without funds
questions.explain: Antifederalists feared distant government and lack of explicit protection for individual rights.

questions.q: The Federalist Papers were written to:
options: argue for independence from Great Britain in 1776
defend the institution of slavery in the South
oppose the creation of the first national bank
persuade New Yorkers to support the Constitution
questions.explain: The essays appeared in New York newspapers in 1787-1788 under the pen name "Publius."

questions.q: Which three men wrote the Federalist Papers?
options: Thomas Jefferson, John Adams, and Benjamin Franklin
George Mason, Patrick Henry, and Richard Henry Lee
Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay
George Washington, Alexander Hamilton, and James Madison
questions.explain: Hamilton wrote most of the 85 essays, Madison about twenty-nine, and Jay five.

questions.q: In Federalist No. 10, James Madison argued that a large republic would:
options: help control the harm caused by factions
give nearly all power to the state governments
make direct democracy possible in every state
eliminate all political parties from public life
questions.explain: Madison believed a large republic with many competing interests would make it harder for one faction to dominate.

questions.q: Federalist No. 51 argues that "ambition must be made to counteract ambition." What idea does this support?
options: Direct election of the president by the people
Rule by a single party with a strong executive
Equal distribution of wealth among all citizens
Checks and balances among branches of government
questions.explain: Madison explained that dividing power and giving each branch the means of resisting others protects liberty.

questions.q: Federalist No. 78 described the judiciary as the "least dangerous" of the three departments because it:
options: collected the taxes that funded all federal salaries
had neither the sword nor the purse and relied on judgment
wrote the laws that all the other branches enforced
controlled the army and directed the national militia
questions.explain: Hamilton argued that courts could safely check legislatures through judicial review because they lacked force or funding.

questions.q: Hamilton's argument in Federalist No. 78 supports which later judicial power?
options: The power to declare war on foreign nations
The power to impeach presidents and senators
The power to appoint ambassadors and ministers
Judicial review of laws for constitutionality
questions.explain: He wrote that judges must treat the Constitution as fundamental law when ordinary statutes conflict with it.

questions.q: Which of these was the pen name of an Antifederalist essayist who warned that the Constitution concentrated too much power in a distant government?
options: Brutus
Common Sense
Publius
Cato Minor
questions.explain: The Brutus essays warned that a large republic and a powerful national government would endanger liberty.

questions.q: Which Virginia orator opposed ratification, saying he "smelt a rat" about the convention?
options: George Mason
Edmund Pendleton
Patrick Henry
John Marshall
questions.explain: Henry feared the Constitution threatened state sovereignty and individual liberties.

questions.q: Antifederalists argued that a bill of rights was needed because:
options: they wanted a king to protect liberties of the people
the Constitution did not guarantee key individual liberties
state constitutions already protected all national rights
they opposed freedom of speech and freedom of the press
questions.explain: Federalists first argued that listing rights was unnecessary, but promised amendments to secure ratification.

questions.q: The Massachusetts ratifying convention of 1788 helped win approval by:
options: rejecting the Constitution until a bill of rights passed
approving it without recommending any changes
demanding that senators be chosen by popular vote first
ratifying while recommending a list of amendments
questions.explain: This "ratify now, amend later" approach was copied by other states and reassured critics.

questions.q: Which state was the first to ratify the Constitution, doing so unanimously in December 1787?
options: Pennsylvania
New Jersey
Delaware
Georgia
questions.explain: Small states like Delaware valued the equal voice they gained in the Senate.

questions.q: The ninth state to ratify the Constitution, putting it into effect, was:
options: Massachusetts
New Hampshire
New York
Virginia
questions.explain: New Hampshire's vote in June 1788 met the threshold, though Virginia and New York soon followed.

questions.q: Why were the ratification decisions of Virginia and New York so important even after nine states approved?
options: They were large states whose loss would weaken the union
They held a majority of seats in the Confederation Congress
They held the only major ports on the Atlantic coast
They owned all of the western lands claimed by states
questions.explain: Without these two states, the union would have been geographically divided and economically weakened.

questions.q: Which two states did not ratify the Constitution until after the new government had begun operating?
options: Virginia and New Hampshire
Maryland and South Carolina
Delaware and Massachusetts
North Carolina and Rhode Island
questions.explain: North Carolina ratified in 1789 and Rhode Island in 1790 after the Bill of Rights was proposed.

questions.q: Federalists such as Madison feared that a bill of rights could:
options: suggest that unlisted rights were not protected
create an office with powers like a king's
prevent states from holding free elections
replace the Constitution with a weaker document
questions.explain: Madison eventually supported amendments to answer critics and secure support in Virginia.

questions.q: The first ten amendments to the Constitution are known as:
options: the Declaration of Rights
the Reconstruction Amendments
the Bill of Rights
the Federalist Amendments
questions.explain: They were ratified in 1791 to guard individual liberties and limit national power.

questions.q: Who drafted the Bill of Rights and guided it through the First Congress?
options: Thomas Jefferson
James Madison
John Adams
Alexander Hamilton
questions.explain: Madison drew on state declarations of rights and proposals offered at ratifying conventions.

questions.q: The Bill of Rights was ratified in what year?
questions.explain: Virginia's vote in December 1791 provided the needed three-fourths of states.

questions.q: Of the amendments Congress sent to the states in 1789, how many were ratified at that time as the Bill of Rights?
options: Eight
Fifteen
Ten
Twelve
questions.explain: The two remaining proposals concerned congressional apportionment and pay; the pay measure became the Twenty-seventh Amendment in 1992.

questions.q: Which amendment protects freedom of speech, press, religion, assembly, and petition?
options: The Second Amendment
The First Amendment
The Fourth Amendment
The Fifth Amendment
questions.explain: The First Amendment guards these rights from interference by Congress.

questions.q: The Third Amendment, which limits quartering soldiers in private homes in peacetime, responded to a grievance from:
options: the colonial period under British rule
the weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation
the later War of 1812 with Britain
the Whiskey Rebellion of the 1790s
questions.explain: Quartering troops without consent was one of the colonists' complaints against Britain.

questions.q: The Fourth Amendment protects against:
options: quartering troops in private homes
double jeopardy in criminal trials
cruel and unusual forms of punishment
unreasonable searches and seizures
questions.explain: It requires warrants based on probable cause for most searches.

questions.q: Which amendment includes the right to a speedy and public trial and to be informed of the accusation?
options: The Sixth Amendment
The Ninth Amendment
The Fifth Amendment
The Eighth Amendment
questions.explain: The Sixth Amendment guarantees an impartial jury, counsel, and the right to confront witnesses.

questions.q: The Fifth Amendment includes protection against:
options: peacetime quartering of soldiers in homes
being forced to testify against oneself
excessive bail demanded by judges
licensing rules imposed on the press
questions.explain: It also includes the grand jury requirement, protection against double jeopardy, and due process.

questions.q: The Eighth Amendment forbids:
options: quartering of troops in private homes during peace
compelled testimony in criminal proceedings
excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishments
unreasonable searches and seizures of property
questions.explain: The language derived from the English Bill of Rights of 1689.

questions.q: The Tenth Amendment states that powers not given to the national government nor prohibited to the states are reserved to:
options: the states or the people
Congress and the courts
the Supreme Court justices
the president and cabinet
questions.explain: This amendment reflects federalism and the idea of limited, enumerated national powers.

questions.q: The Ninth Amendment says that listing certain rights in the Constitution does not mean:
options: the states have no reserved rights of their own
the president may add new rights by executive order
the listed rights may be limited by Congress
other rights retained by the people are denied
questions.explain: It answers the concern that a list of rights might be read as exhaustive.

questions.q: Which English charter, sealed by King John in 1215, influenced American ideas of due process and limits on rulers?
options: The Petition of Right
Magna Carta
The Domesday Book
The Mayflower Compact
questions.explain: Magna Carta established that even the king was subject to law, a principle echoed in American documents.

questions.q: The National Archives displays the Declaration, the Constitution, and the Bill of Rights in a space known as the:
options: Jefferson Wing for the Founding Papers
Gallery of the Presidents' Papers
Rotunda for the Charters of Freedom
Senate Gallery of Founding Documents
questions.explain: These documents are displayed in the Rotunda of the National Archives Building.

questions.q: Which document, displayed at the National Archives, begins "We the People of the United States, in Order to form a more perfect Union"?
options: The Declaration of Independence
The Constitution
The Articles of Confederation
The Bill of Rights
questions.explain: The Preamble introduces the Constitution's purposes, including justice, domestic tranquility, and liberty.

questions.q: The first Congress under the Constitution met in 1789 in which city?
options: Boston
Philadelphia
New York City
Washington
