questions.explain: Congress met at Federal Hall in New York before moving to Philadelphia in 1790.

questions.q: George Washington took the presidential oath of office on April 30, 1789 in:
options: Philadelphia
Mount Vernon
Washington, D.C.
New York City
questions.explain: He was inaugurated on the balcony of Federal Hall, the first capitol building under the Constitution.

questions.q: Washington was elected president in 1788-1789 by:
options: a unanimous vote of the electors
a vote by the House
a majority of the popular vote only
a narrow margin
questions.explain: Washington received every elector's vote in both 1789 and 1792, and John Adams became vice president.

questions.q: Who served as the first vice president?
options: Aaron Burr
John Adams
John Jay
Thomas Jefferson
questions.explain: Adams finished second in the electoral vote and presided over the Senate.

questions.q: Who served as the first Speaker of the House of Representatives?
options: James Madison
Fisher Ames
Jonathan Trumbull Jr.
Frederick Muhlenberg
questions.explain: Muhlenberg of Pennsylvania held the post in the First Congress and in the Third.

questions.q: Which law first organized the federal court system?
options: The Judiciary Act of 1789
The Naturalization Act
The Judiciary Act of 1801
The Alien Act
questions.explain: It created district and circuit courts and defined the structure of the Supreme Court.

questions.q: How many justices did the Judiciary Act of 1789 establish for the Supreme Court?
options: Twelve
Nine
Six
Three
questions.explain: The size was set at six and was later changed by Congress; nine has been the number since 1869.

questions.q: Under the Judiciary Act of 1789, justices of the Supreme Court also:
options: presided over the Senate on days of heavy debate
commanded state militias during emergencies
rode circuit to hear cases in different regions
served as members of the president's cabinet
questions.explain: Circuit riding burdened justices with long travel and was a source of complaint for years.

questions.q: Chisholm v. Georgia (1793) caused controversy because the Court held that:
options: states could not tax goods imported from other states
states could be sued by citizens of other states
the president could remove federal judges at will
federal courts could review every state criminal case
questions.explain: The decision alarmed the states and led to the Eleventh Amendment, ratified in 1795.

questions.q: The Eleventh Amendment, ratified in 1795, was a response to:
options: Chisholm v. Georgia
McCulloch v. Maryland
Marbury v. Madison
Hylton v. United States
questions.explain: It limited federal courts' power to hear suits against states by citizens of other states or countries.

questions.q: Hylton v. United States (1796) is notable because the Supreme Court:
options: rejected the national bank's charter as unconstitutional
allowed states to tax the property of federal officials
struck down a state law taxing imported goods
upheld a carriage tax as not being a direct tax
questions.explain: The Court's first major review of a federal law's constitutionality did not strike down the law.

questions.q: The federal court system created by Congress in 1789 relied on lower federal courts, which the Constitution:
options: gave to the states to organize and control
forbade outright to prevent conflicts with states
required by name in the text of Article III
allowed Congress to create but did not require
questions.explain: Article III set up one Supreme Court and allowed Congress to establish inferior courts.

questions.q: The president's cabinet is not described in the Constitution except for the idea that:
options: cabinet members hold a vote to decide questions of policy
the Senate directly supervises each executive department
the president may seek written opinions from department heads
the president must appoint exactly five department secretaries
questions.explain: Washington's cabinet developed by custom, led by Jefferson at State and Hamilton at Treasury.

questions.q: Washington's first Secretary of State was:
options: Alexander Hamilton
Thomas Jefferson
Edmund Randolph
Henry Knox
questions.explain: Jefferson returned from France in 1789 to serve in the post.

questions.q: Washington's first Secretary of the Treasury was:
options: Alexander Hamilton
Thomas Jefferson
Albert Gallatin
Robert Morris
questions.explain: Hamilton led the effort to stabilize the new nation's finances.

questions.q: Henry Knox, Washington's Secretary of War, had earlier gained fame for:
options: negotiating the terms of the treaty ending the war with Britain
moving captured cannon from Fort Ticonderoga to Boston
leading the farmers who closed courts in Massachusetts
writing several of the essays in the Federalist Papers
questions.explain: Knox's artillery helped force the British out of Boston in 1776.

questions.q: Edmund Randolph served Washington as the first:
options: Secretary of War
Postmaster General
Attorney General
Chief Justice
questions.explain: Randolph, a Virginian who had presented the Virginia Plan at the convention, served as the first U.S. attorney general.

questions.q: Washington's use of a small advisory group of department heads set a precedent for:
options: the Electoral College
the Supreme Court
the House committee system
the presidential cabinet
questions.explain: The practice of consulting the cabinet grew into an enduring tradition.

questions.q: By stepping down after two terms in 1797, Washington established a tradition that lasted until:
options: Franklin D. Roosevelt's third election in 1940
Ulysses S. Grant's second election in 1872
Andrew Jackson's reelection to the presidency
Abraham Lincoln's second election in 1864
questions.explain: The two-term custom was formalized in the Twenty-second Amendment in 1951.

questions.q: Alexander Hamilton's first major proposal as Treasury Secretary, in 1790, was to:
options: replace the dollar with a British currency
pay the national debt in full at face value
cancel the debt owed to foreign nations
print paper money without any backing
questions.explain: Hamilton argued that honoring the debt would build the credit of the new government at home and abroad.

questions.q: Hamilton's plan for "assumption" meant that the national government would:
options: pay the states for their wartime militia service
require the states to repay money they owed Congress
take over the Revolutionary War debts of the states
forgive the debts the nation owed to Britain
questions.explain: Assumption bound state creditors to the federal government and reduced the states' independent power.

questions.q: Which states were most opposed to Hamilton's plan to assume state debts?
options: Southern states such as Virginia that had paid most debts
Western settlements that had no debts to report at all
New England states that carried the largest unpaid debts
Mid-Atlantic merchants who held large amounts of bonds
questions.explain: Virginia and others had already paid much of their debts and objected to subsidizing states that had not.

questions.q: The Compromise of 1790 combined Hamilton's assumption plan with a decision about:
options: ending the Atlantic slave trade by federal law
opening the Mississippi River to American shipping
creating a federal Supreme Court of six justices
locating the permanent capital on the Potomac River
questions.explain: Jefferson, Madison, and Hamilton reportedly struck the bargain at a dinner, and the capital was placed in the South.

questions.q: Which institution did Congress charter in 1791 to hold government funds and issue a national currency?
options: The Second Continental Treasury
The Mint of Philadelphia
The Bank of the United States
The Federal Reserve
questions.explain: The first Bank of the United States received a twenty-year charter and was based in Philadelphia.

questions.q: Hamilton defended the constitutionality of the national bank using the idea of:
options: implied powers drawn from the "necessary and proper" clause
the Tenth Amendment's reservation of powers to the states
the principle of popular sovereignty in the Preamble
the Declaration's language about natural rights
questions.explain: Hamilton argued that creating a bank was a means to carry out powers like collecting taxes and borrowing money.

questions.q: The disagreement between Hamilton and Jefferson over the bank is an example of the debate between:
options: free trade and protection for American manufacturing
strict construction and loose construction of the Constitution
state sovereignty and national supremacy in foreign policy
republican government and constitutional monarchy in America
questions.explain: Their dispute shaped later arguments about the scope of federal power.

questions.q: Hamilton's Report on Manufactures (1791) recommended that the government:
options: give federal land grants only to western farmers
encourage industry with tariffs and government bounties
ban the construction of factories in coastal cities
end all duties on imports to promote free trade abroad
questions.explain: The report was a vision for a diverse economy, though Congress adopted few of its proposals at the time.

questions.q: The 1791 excise tax on distilled spirits was intended mainly to:
options: raise revenue to help pay the debts
protect British exports
reduce drinking among settlers
punish western farmers
questions.explain: The tax helped fund the assumed debts but angered farmers in the backcountry.

questions.q: Hamilton's financial program mostly benefited and was supported by:
options: artisans, sailors, and laborers in the port towns
small farmers and debtors in the western counties
southern plantation owners and tobacco exporters
merchants, bankers, and holders of public securities
questions.explain: His plan tied the interests of wealthy investors to the new government, which Jefferson's supporters criticized.

questions.q: The Coinage Act (Mint Act) of 1792 established:
options: a tax on silver mining in the western territories
a ban on foreign coins from circulating in the states
a national mint and a decimal system for coins
a new charter for the national bank in Philadelphia
questions.explain: The mint was located in Philadelphia and the dollar became the unit of account, divided by tens.

questions.q: The Coinage Act of 1792 put the United States on what kind of metallic standard?
options: A gold-only standard
A bimetallic standard using both gold and silver
A silver-only standard
A standard tied to the British pound
questions.explain: The act defined the dollar in both silver and gold and set a ratio between them, a bimetallic standard that lasted into the 1800s.

questions.q: Hamilton's plan to "fund" the debt meant that government would:
options: confiscate private property to pay off creditors
tax only the wealthiest citizens until the debt was repaid
pay all bondholders at once in gold and silver coins
issue new bonds and pay interest on them over time
questions.explain: Funding turned the old debt into a regular obligation secured by tariff and excise revenue.

questions.q: The Tariff Act of 1789, one of the first major laws passed by Congress, was meant to:
options: end trade with Britain and strengthen ties with France
raise revenue and give some protection to U.S. industry
ban all foreign ships from entering American harbors
pay the salaries of state judges across the country
questions.explain: The tariff gave the new government a dependable source of funds.

questions.q: The Whiskey Rebellion (1791-1794) in western Pennsylvania was a protest against:
options: a federal excise tax on whiskey
the national bank charter
a tariff on British goods
a ban on western settlement
questions.explain: Farmers who turned grain into whiskey resisted the tax, harassing tax collectors.

questions.q: Washington's response to the Whiskey Rebellion demonstrated that:
options: federal tax laws could be ignored without consequence
the states could nullify federal laws they disliked
state militias would refuse to obey federal orders
the federal government could enforce its laws by force
questions.explain: He personally led militia toward Pennsylvania, and the protest collapsed without a major battle.

questions.q: About how many militiamen did Washington assemble to suppress the Whiskey Rebellion?
options: About 50,000
About 300
About 13,000
About 2,000
questions.explain: The force, led in part by Washington himself, was meant to show federal strength.

questions.q: Critics of Washington's handling of the Whiskey Rebellion argued that it showed:
options: an overreaction to citizens exercising a right to protest
support for state sovereignty over federal taxation
weakness in dealing with the British over frontier forts
bias toward the western farmers' side of the dispute
questions.explain: Democratic-Republicans saw the show of force as proof of Federalist heavy-handedness.

questions.q: The Naturalization Act of 1790 allowed which immigrants to become citizens?
options: Any free person after five years of continuous residence
Free white persons after two years of residence
All people born abroad upon arrival at a port city
Only landowners born in Britain after seven years
questions.explain: The act limited naturalization to free white persons, excluding enslaved people, free Black people, and later Asian immigrants.

questions.q: The Fugitive Slave Act of 1793 gave slaveholders the legal right to:
options: take enslaved people into free territory and keep them
vote on abolition within their own state legislatures
seize and return people who had escaped to another state
sue the federal government for the loss of property
questions.explain: The act implemented the Constitution's clause and weakened protection for free Black people in the North.

questions.q: Eli Whitney's cotton gin, patented in 1794, changed the South by:
options: reducing the South's need for enslaved workers on plantations
making short-staple cotton profitable and boosting slavery
cutting cotton prices in half across the Atlantic world
shifting most cotton growing to New England farms
questions.explain: The machine sped up cleaning of seeds, spreading cotton cultivation and slavery across the Deep South.

questions.q: Samuel Slater, who built a water-powered cotton spinning mill in Rhode Island in 1790, is often called:
options: the father of the American factory system
the first banker of New England merchants
the inventor of the practical steam engine
the founder of the Erie Canal project
questions.explain: Slater, a British immigrant who had worked in English textile mills, reproduced the technology in the United States.

questions.q: In 1790, Quaker petitions and one signed by Benjamin Franklin asked the First Congress to:
options: abolish the Senate in favor of a single house
create an official state church for the nation
ban Catholic immigration into the new republic
take steps against slavery and the slave trade
questions.explain: Congress responded that it could not ban the slave trade before 1808 and had no authority to interfere with emancipation or the treatment of slaves within the states.

questions.q: The First Congress responded to the antislavery petitions of 1790 by:
options: declaring that it could not act on slavery in the states
ending the international slave trade immediately
levying a national tax on slaveholders and traders
passing a law ending slavery in all northern states
questions.explain: The debate revealed sectional divisions over slavery within the new government.

questions.q: Which early Black institution, founded in Philadelphia by Richard Allen and Absalom Jones in 1787, aided free Black communities?
options: The African Free School
The American Colonization Society
The Free African Society
The Freedmen's Bureau
questions.explain: It offered mutual aid and became a model for later Black churches and societies.

questions.q: The Haitian Revolution (1791-1804) affected the United States by:
options: ending all American trade with the French colonies
ending the slave trade into the United States at once
bringing Spain into an alliance against France
alarming slaveholders and bringing refugees to port cities
questions.explain: News of the successful revolt inspired enslaved people and alarmed slaveholders, while thousands of refugees came to American ports.

questions.q: Which formerly enslaved general became the leading figure of the Haitian Revolution in the 1790s and was captured by the French in 1802?
options: Napoleon Bonaparte
Toussaint Louverture
Simon Bolivar
Jean-Jacques Dessalines
questions.explain: Louverture led the rebellion in Saint-Domingue; Dessalines declared Haiti independent in 1804.

questions.q: Gabriel's Rebellion of 1800 in Virginia was:
options: a revolt by Loyalist militia against the Virginia government
a strike by dock workers in Norfolk and Richmond over wages
a protest by free farmers against a new state tax
an uprising planned near Richmond and discovered early
questions.explain: Gabriel and others were executed, and Virginia tightened its slave laws.

questions.q: What did George Washington's will direct about the enslaved people he owned?
options: He divided them among his heirs as part of his estate
He ordered those he owned freed after Martha's death
He directed that they be sold to pay his remaining debts
He ordered every one of them freed on the day of his death
questions.explain: Washington's will freed those he owned, and Martha Washington freed them in 1801; the Custis dower slaves were not freed.

questions.q: Washington's Neutrality Proclamation of 1793 declared that the United States would:
options: remain neutral in the war between Britain and France
join France's war against Britain under the 1778 treaty
support Britain in its war against revolutionary France
side with Spain in a war over the Mississippi River
questions.explain: Washington sought to keep the weak young nation out of European conflict.

questions.q: Some critics, including Madison, argued that Washington's Neutrality Proclamation overstepped because:
options: it increased the size of the army without Congress
it formally sided with Britain over revolutionary France
it appeared to usurp Congress's war and treaty powers
it damaged the national bank's ability to lend money
questions.explain: Hamilton defended it as part of the executive's power to conduct foreign relations.

questions.q: The Genet Affair of 1793 involved a French diplomat who:
options: asked the United States to return lands taken from France
tried to enlist Americans against Britain despite neutrality
declared war on Spain from the port of Charleston
demanded a new treaty giving France trade preference
questions.explain: Washington demanded his recall; he stayed in the United States to avoid the guillotine.

questions.q: Jay's Treaty (1794) with Britain resulted in:
options: an alliance against France
payment for enslaved people freed during the war
British withdrawal from Northwest forts
an end to British impressment
questions.explain: The treaty left other issues unresolved, such as impressment and some trade restrictions.

questions.q: Why did Jay's Treaty become so controversial?
options: It gave too much to Britain and ignored impressment
It was signed before the Senate could review any draft
It allowed French privateers to use American ports freely
It declared war on Britain over frontier forts and debts
questions.explain: Opponents burned Jay in effigy, but the Senate narrowly ratified it in 1795.

questions.q: The Senate ratified Jay's Treaty by exactly:
options: a bare simple majority of the Senate
a vote of the House of Representatives
a unanimous vote of every senator
the two-thirds majority required
questions.explain: The vote was 20 to 10, just meeting the constitutional threshold.

questions.q: Jay's Treaty also led to a dispute in the House over:
options: whether the House could demand papers and vote on funding the treaty
whether senators should be elected directly by the people
whether Congress could declare war on Britain over impressment
whether Washington could hold a third term in office
questions.explain: The House demanded diplomatic documents and Washington refused, asserting executive privilege.

questions.q: Pinckney's Treaty of 1795 with Spain gave Americans:
options: control of the Louisiana territory west of the river
a military alliance with Spain against Great Britain
outright ownership of the Spanish colony of East Florida
the right to navigate the Mississippi and trade at New Orleans
questions.explain: The agreement boosted western farmers and settled the southern boundary at the 31st parallel.

questions.q: The Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794) was a victory for American forces led by:
options: General Josiah Harmar
General Arthur St. Clair
General Anthony Wayne
General Henry Knox
questions.explain: Wayne's forces defeated the Western Confederacy near present-day Toledo, Ohio.

questions.q: The Treaty of Greenville (1795) required Native nations of the Northwest to:
options: give up all of their lands east of the Mississippi River
cede most of present-day Ohio and parts of Indiana
move permanently to Canada under British protection
submit to British authority at the Northwest forts
questions.explain: After their defeat at Fallen Timbers in 1794, Native nations signed the Treaty of Greenville, ceding most of present-day Ohio and parts of Indiana and opening the land to settlers.

questions.q: Before Fallen Timbers, American armies led by Harmar and St. Clair were defeated in the early 1790s by:
options: Spanish soldiers advancing north from New Orleans
French volunteers sent by the revolutionary government
a Native confederacy led by Little Turtle and Blue Jacket
British regulars sent south from the forts in Canada
questions.explain: St. Clair's 1791 defeat on the Wabash was one of the worst ever suffered by the U.S. Army.

questions.q: In the 1790s, the Washington administration's treaties with Native nations were meant to:
options: treat nations as sovereign but acquire land through treaties
grant Native nations seats in the House of Representatives
make Native people citizens of the nearest state at once
remove all Native nations from east of the Mississippi
questions.explain: Policy often promised protection of borders but treaties were repeatedly broken by settlers and governments.

questions.q: Washington's Farewell Address of 1796 warned Americans against:
options: renewing the charter of the Bank of the United States
holding elections for the presidency every four years
building a permanent navy to defend overseas trade
permanent alliances with foreign nations
questions.explain: He urged the nation to expand trade but avoid binding political ties to Europe.

questions.q: In his Farewell Address, Washington cautioned that political parties could:
options: strengthen the states against the federal government
divide the nation and invite foreign influence
lower taxes by keeping government small and local
improve the quality of elections through competition
questions.explain: He feared factions would put party interests above the common good.

questions.q: Each year on or near February 22, the Senate honors Washington's birthday by:
options: reciting the Declaration
electing a new vice president
reading aloud his Farewell Address
voting on a new bill
questions.explain: The tradition began in 1862 during the Civil War to inspire unity.

questions.q: Washington's Farewell Address was first published:
options: in a pamphlet printed for sale in London and Paris
as a newspaper essay rather than as a speech
as a letter privately sent to each state governor
in a speech delivered to a joint session of Congress
questions.explain: He chose to release it in the American Daily Advertiser in September 1796.

questions.q: Washington's decision not to seek a third term in 1796 helped establish:
options: the Electoral College system for presidential elections
the rule of Congress over the executive branch
a lasting ban on organized political parties
the precedent of the voluntary transfer of power
questions.explain: His retirement showed that the president was an officeholder, not a monarch.

questions.q: Henry Lee's famous eulogy for Washington described him as:
options: first in war, first in peace, and first in the hearts of his countrymen
the greatest of the Founders and the model of republican virtue
first in command, first in wisdom, and first in the esteem of Europe
the savior of the republic and the father of the Constitution
questions.explain: Lee delivered the line after Washington's death in December 1799.

questions.q: Washington died in December 1799 at:
options: Alexandria
Mount Vernon
Williamsburg
Philadelphia
questions.explain: Washington died at Mount Vernon, his Virginia plantation, on December 14, 1799, after a brief throat illness.

questions.q: By the mid-1790s two political groups had formed: the Federalists and the:
options: Democratic-Republicans
Know-Nothing Party
Free Soil Party
National Republicans
questions.explain: Jefferson and Madison led the opposition party that favored states' rights and agrarian interests.

questions.q: Which leader is most associated with the Federalist Party?
options: Aaron Burr
Thomas Jefferson
James Madison
Alexander Hamilton
questions.explain: Hamilton favored a strong central government and commercial development.

questions.q: Democratic-Republicans generally supported:
options: an official national church and a hereditary Senate
a strong national bank and warm ties with Britain
a limited national government and sympathy for France
a large standing army and high protective tariffs
questions.explain: They saw the Federalists as too friendly to Britain and to wealthy interests.

questions.q: Federalists drew much of their strength from:
options: merchants and creditors in the Northeast
debtors living in the backcountry counties
small farmers in the western settlements
plantation owners across the Deep South
questions.explain: The Federalists, led by Alexander Hamilton, drew strength from Northeastern merchants and creditors, who favored a strong central government, a national bank and close trade ties with Britain.

questions.q: Democratic-Republican societies of the 1790s were groups that:
options: condemned the French Revolution and its supporters
recruited soldiers for Wayne's campaign in the Northwest
attacked Washington's policies and urged public voice
defended the national bank and Hamilton's financial plan
questions.explain: Washington blamed them for stirring up the Whiskey Rebellion.

questions.q: Which foreign event most sharply divided Americans into Federalists and Democratic-Republicans in the 1790s?
options: The Congress of Vienna and the new European order
The Napoleonic Code and the French legal reforms
The Haitian Revolution and the end of the slave trade
The French Revolution and its wars with Britain
questions.explain: Democratic-Republicans sympathized with France while Federalists leaned toward Britain.

questions.q: Who won the presidential election of 1796?
options: Alexander Hamilton
John Adams
Thomas Jefferson
Aaron Burr
questions.explain: Federalist John Adams narrowly won the 1796 election, 71 electoral votes to 68 for Thomas Jefferson, who became vice president under the rules of the time.

questions.q: In 1796, Thomas Jefferson became vice president under John Adams because:
options: Adams personally selected him as his running mate
the voters elected him separately in a second contest
Congress selected him after counting the votes
the runner-up in electoral votes became vice president
questions.explain: The system before the Twelfth Amendment produced a divided executive.

questions.q: John Adams is best known for his role in the Revolution as:
options: a Loyalist writer who defended royal authority
the commander who accepted Cornwallis's surrender
a congressional leader who pushed for independence
a general who led the American army at Saratoga
questions.explain: Adams championed independence in Congress and nominated Washington to lead the army.

questions.q: The XYZ Affair (1797-98) was a diplomatic incident in which French agents:
options: demanded that Congress declare war on Britain
demanded bribes before talks with American envoys
attacked an American merchant ship in the harbor
seized American territory near the Mississippi
questions.explain: The scandal angered Americans and increased support for war preparations.

questions.q: The Quasi-War of 1798-1800 was an undeclared naval conflict between the United States and:
options: France
Spain
Britain
Algiers
questions.explain: Ships clashed in the Caribbean while Congress built up the navy.

questions.q: Congress created the Department of the Navy in 1798 in response to:
options: Spanish raids along the southern frontier
French attacks on American merchant shipping
the Whiskey Rebellion in western Pennsylvania
the terms of the Jay Treaty with Britain
questions.explain: A larger navy was seen as necessary to protect commerce during the Quasi-War.

questions.q: During the Quasi-War, President Adams surprised some Federalists by:
options: asking Congress to declare war on France
ordering the navy to blockade French ports in Europe
forming a military alliance with Great Britain
seeking a peaceful settlement with France
questions.explain: Adams sent new envoys and later considered it one of his best decisions.

questions.q: The Convention of 1800 (Treaty of Mortefontaine) ended:
options: the 1778 alliance and the Quasi-War with France
the Whiskey Rebellion and the militia call-up
the Barbary conflicts and tribute payments
the Jay Treaty and the dispute with Britain
questions.explain: The agreement freed the U.S. from the 1778 alliance, though it cost Adams political support.

questions.q: The Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798 were passed by a Congress controlled by:
options: Republicans of 1860
Whigs
Federalists
Democratic-Republicans
questions.explain: Federalists said the laws protected national security during the Quasi-War.

questions.q: The Sedition Act of 1798 made it a crime to:
options: print false or malicious writing against the government
vote more than once in a federal election
publish criticism of any foreign monarch in print
sell military supplies to the French government
questions.explain: Critics said it targeted Democratic-Republican newspaper editors and violated the First Amendment.

questions.q: The Naturalization Act of 1798 increased the residency requirement for citizenship from five to:
options: twenty years
seven years
ten years
fourteen years
questions.explain: Federalists wanted to slow the influence of immigrants, who often supported the Democratic-Republicans.

questions.q: The Alien Act of 1798 gave the president power to:
options: seize foreign ships entering American ports
deport noncitizens considered dangerous
ban all immigration from foreign nations
end the process of naturalization entirely
questions.explain: The Alien Act let the president deport noncitizens he judged dangerous to the country. Adams never used it, but it alarmed immigrants and critics of his administration.

questions.q: Matthew Lyon, a Vermont congressman, was convicted under the Sedition Act for:
options: giving military secrets to French agents
refusing to pay the new direct tax
writing criticism of President Adams
leading a protest against the federal tax
questions.explain: Matthew Lyon was convicted under the Sedition Act for writing criticism of President Adams. He was jailed and won reelection to Congress while still in prison.

questions.q: Supporters of the Sedition Act argued that it was constitutional because:
options: it punished false statements, as common law allowed
the First Amendment explicitly permitted such laws
the state legislatures had required Congress to pass it
it applied only to foreigners living in the nation
questions.explain: Federalists said the First Amendment barred prior restraint but not punishing libel after publication.

questions.q: The Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions of 1798-1799 argued that:
options: only federal courts could ever decide such questions
states could judge the constitutionality of federal laws
Congress had to obey instructions from state governors
the president could ban newspapers critical of him
questions.explain: Jefferson wrote the Kentucky Resolutions and Madison wrote Virginia's, to protest the Alien and Sedition Acts.

questions.q: Which Founders secretly wrote the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions?
options: John Adams and Alexander Hamilton
George Washington and John Jay
Patrick Henry and George Mason
Thomas Jefferson and James Madison
questions.explain: They worked secretly because Jefferson was vice president when the resolutions were drafted.

questions.q: The Kentucky Resolutions introduced the idea of:
options: executive privilege for withholding papers from Congress
judicial review of acts of Congress by the courts
nullification, a state's power to void a federal law
popular election of senators by voters of each state
questions.explain: Jefferson's draft called nullification the rightful remedy. Other states did not endorse the idea, but it resurfaced in later crises.

questions.q: How did the other states respond to the resolutions of Kentucky and Virginia?
options: Several rejected them, and none endorsed nullification
They passed identical resolutions in their legislatures
Every one of them approved and passed matching resolutions
They threatened Virginia and Kentucky with military action
questions.explain: Northern legislatures generally replied that the courts, not states, decide constitutionality.

questions.q: Federalist critics of the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions argued that:
options: the president alone has the power to decide what is lawful
federal courts, not states, interpret the Constitution
Congress alone decides on the constitutionality of its laws
state governors decide whether federal laws are valid
questions.explain: This view foreshadowed the later doctrine of judicial review.

questions.q: Fries's Rebellion of 1799 in Pennsylvania was a protest against:
options: the new Navy Department and its construction costs
a federal excise tax on whiskey and distilled spirits
the Alien Act's deportation power over foreigners
a federal tax on houses, land, and enslaved people
questions.explain: John Fries led resistance to assessors, and Adams pardoned him.

questions.q: The presidential election of 1800 ended in a tie between Thomas Jefferson and:
options: John Adams
Alexander Hamilton
Aaron Burr
Charles Pinckney
questions.explain: Both Democratic-Republican candidates received 73 electoral votes.

questions.q: Who decided the tied election of 1800?
options: The Supreme Court by special ruling
The Electoral College in a second vote
The Senate by a vote of its members
The House of Representatives
questions.explain: The House voted by state delegations and chose Jefferson on the 36th ballot in February 1801.

questions.q: The Twelfth Amendment, ratified in 1804, fixed the problem exposed in 1800 by requiring:
options: separate electoral ballots for the two offices
a runoff election between the two leading candidates
a single term of six years for every president
direct election of the president by all voters
questions.explain: The amendment prevented a repeat of the tie between running mates.

questions.q: Hamilton's influence in the 1800 House vote helped Jefferson because:
options: he feared that the voters would decide the election
he wanted Adams to win another term in office
he considered Jefferson less dangerous than Burr
he sympathized with the French Revolution
questions.explain: Hamilton distrusted Burr's ambition and urged Federalists to choose Jefferson.

questions.q: The peaceful transfer of power from the Federalists to the Democratic-Republicans in 1801 is sometimes called:
options: the Jeffersonian Reaction
the Revolution of 1800
the Glorious Revolution
the Era of Good Feelings
questions.explain: Jefferson himself used the term for a change achieved by votes rather than violence.

questions.q: Jefferson's first inaugural address in 1801 stressed unity with the line "We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists," which meant:
options: only Republicans would serve in his government
he intended to abolish all political parties
the Federalists were enemies of the republic
disagreements are not differences of principle
questions.explain: Jefferson tried to calm the bitter election and reassure the losing side.

questions.q: Adams' last-minute appointments of Federalist judges were made under:
options: the Embargo Act
the Judiciary Act of 1801
the Judiciary Act of 1789
the Naturalization Act
questions.explain: These "midnight judges" filled new circuit courts. Adams's related last-minute D.C. justice-of-the-peace commissions, made under a separate 1801 law, led to Marbury v. Madison in 1803.

questions.q: The "midnight judges" controversy at the end of Adams' presidency illustrates:
options: a partisan struggle over control of the judiciary
a dispute over slavery in the new territories
a conflict over the national bank's charter
a debate over the location of the capital
questions.explain: Adams filled new judgeships created by the Judiciary Act of 1801 with Federalists in his final days. Republicans repealed the act in 1802, and the fight led to Marbury v. Madison.

questions.q: The Residence Act of 1790 chose to locate the permanent national capital:
options: on the Delaware River
on the Susquehanna River
on the Potomac River
on the Hudson River
questions.explain: The act authorized the president to select a site along the Potomac and made Philadelphia the temporary capital.

questions.q: Under the Residence Act of 1790, which city served as the temporary capital for ten years?
options: Boston
New York
Baltimore
Philadelphia
questions.explain: The Residence Act made Philadelphia the temporary capital while the new federal city was built. Congress met there from 1790 until 1800, when it moved to Washington.

questions.q: Who selected the exact site for the federal district along the Potomac?
options: Alexander Hamilton
James Madison
George Washington
Thomas Jefferson
questions.explain: Washington chose the location in 1791, a location he knew well from his Virginia home.

questions.q: Washington's choice of the Potomac site was influenced by his belief that:
options: it offered the only deepwater port on the coast
the river could link the capital to the west
it was the oldest settled city in the country
it was the nearest available site to Philadelphia
questions.explain: Washington saw the Potomac as a gateway to Ohio Country trade.

questions.q: The federal district was originally laid out as a square measuring:
options: ten miles on each side
one mile on each side
fifty miles on each side
twenty-five miles on each side
questions.explain: The district took land from Maryland and Virginia; Virginia's part was returned in 1846.

questions.q: In what year was the Virginia portion of the original District of Columbia returned to Virginia?
questions.explain: In 1846 Congress returned the area south of the Potomac, including Alexandria, to Virginia. Many residents wanted it, partly to protect the slave trade there.

questions.q: Who prepared the original 1791 plan for the city of Washington?
options: James Hoban
Pierre L'Enfant
William Thornton
Andrew Ellicott
questions.explain: L'Enfant, a French-born engineer, designed a city with broad avenues and diagonal streets.

questions.q: L'Enfant's plan was inspired in part by:
options: European capitals such as Paris and Versailles
the winding medieval streets of old London
the village greens of colonial New England
the grid towns of Spanish colonial America
questions.explain: Pierre L'Enfant drew on European capitals such as Paris and Versailles, laying grand diagonal avenues that radiate from important buildings and public squares.

questions.q: In L'Enfant's plan, which building was placed on a prominent rise called Jenkins Hill?
options: The White House
The Mint
The Treasury
The Capitol
questions.explain: L'Enfant placed the Capitol on Jenkins Hill, now Capitol Hill. He called the hill "a pedestal waiting for a monument."

questions.q: L'Enfant's design separated the Capitol and the President's House along:
options: Constitution Avenue
Pennsylvania Avenue
Independence Avenue
Massachusetts Avenue
questions.explain: Pennsylvania Avenue runs diagonally between the Capitol and the President's House, linking the legislative and executive branches while keeping them apart.

questions.q: L'Enfant was dismissed in 1792 after he:
options: clashed with the commissioners overseeing the city
was accused of spying for the French government
lost the original plan during a move to Philadelphia
abandoned the project to return home to France
questions.explain: He refused to obey the commissioners and demolished a house in the path of a planned street.

questions.q: L'Enfant is buried in:
options: Rock Creek Cemetery in the capital
Mount Vernon in Virginia
Arlington National Cemetery
the crypt beneath the Capitol
questions.explain: His remains were moved to Arlington in 1909 and rest below a view of the city he planned.

questions.q: Benjamin Banneker, a free Black mathematician, helped:
options: write a draft of the Constitution for the convention
found the first library for the Congress of the nation
design the plans for the President's House and gardens
survey the boundaries of the new federal district
questions.explain: Banneker assisted Andrew Ellicott in the survey and published almanacs.

questions.q: In a 1791 letter to Thomas Jefferson, Banneker argued that:
options: Congress should end slavery in every state by the year 1800
Black people were unfit for full citizenship in the republic
Black people had equal talents and slavery betrayed American ideals
the capital should be placed in a southern state to protect slavery
questions.explain: He sent an almanac as proof of intellectual ability and called on Jefferson to support abolition.

questions.q: Which surveyor was officially in charge of the survey of the federal district boundaries?
options: James Hoban
Benjamin Banneker
Pierre L'Enfant
Andrew Ellicott
questions.explain: Ellicott completed the survey and placed boundary stones, many of which still stand.

questions.q: Who designed the White House, then called the President's House?
options: William Thornton
James Hoban
Thomas Jefferson
Pierre L'Enfant
questions.explain: Hoban, an Irish-born architect, won a design competition in 1792.

questions.q: The White House cornerstone was laid in:
questions.explain: The White House cornerstone was laid in October 1792. Architect James Hoban oversaw construction, and John Adams became the first president to live there in 1800.

questions.q: Much of the labor in building the White House and the Capitol was done by:
options: enslaved and free Black workers and immigrant craftsmen
hired European soldiers brought in after the war
only skilled white workers hired from Philadelphia
Native American laborers working under federal contracts
questions.explain: The commissioners hired enslaved laborers from local owners, and skilled craftsmen came from abroad.

questions.q: The Capitol's cornerstone was laid by George Washington in:
questions.explain: Washington took part in a Masonic ceremony on September 18, 1793.

questions.q: The design of the Capitol chosen by Washington in 1793 was by:
options: Thomas Jefferson
James Hoban
Benjamin Latrobe
William Thornton
questions.explain: Thornton, a physician and amateur architect, won the competition with a design Washington admired.

questions.q: The federal city was named in honor of Washington by:
options: Jefferson in a letter of 1801
the commissioners in 1791
Congress in an act of 1800
L'Enfant on his plan in 1790
questions.explain: The commissioners named the federal city "Washington" and the district "Columbia."

questions.q: In what year did the federal government move to Washington, D.C.?
questions.explain: The federal government moved to Washington, D.C., in 1800. Congress first met in the unfinished Capitol that November, and John Adams moved into the President's House.

questions.q: Which president was the first to live in the White House, moving in during 1800?
options: John Adams
James Madison
Thomas Jefferson
George Washington
questions.explain: Adams arrived in November 1800 when the building was unfinished.

questions.q: George Washington never lived in the White House because:
options: he was a slaveholder
it was not completed until 1800
it burned before he arrived
he refused to live there
questions.explain: Washington oversaw its planning, but he died in 1799 before the move.

questions.q: Congress first met in the new Capitol, in the north wing, in:
options: April 1790
July 1814
November 1800
March 1801
questions.explain: Members moved in after Philadelphia and met in the incomplete building.

questions.q: The Library of Congress was founded in 1800 to:
options: store the government's historic archives
educate the general public in the capital
train young lawyers for the new courts
provide books for members of Congress
questions.explain: President Adams signed the act that moved the government and set aside $5,000 for books.

questions.q: The first Library of Congress was housed in:
options: the Capitol
the Treasury
the White House
the Supreme Court
questions.explain: The library was located in the Capitol until moving to its own building in 1897.

questions.q: L'Enfant's plan designated a site for a "great church for national purposes," which suggests that he thought:
options: a king would eventually reside in the capital
the Capitol itself should be turned into a church
the capital should have a national place of worship
a state church would be created for the whole nation
questions.explain: The idea was never carried out by the federal government; the Washington National Cathedral was built later with private funds.

questions.q: Compared to Philadelphia and New York, early Washington, D.C. in 1800 was:
options: the biggest and richest city in all of America
a small, rough, partly built city of mud streets
a fortified military base ringed by new barracks
a large seaport with a mint and busy wharves
questions.explain: Visitors described scattered buildings and few residents, with the Capitol and President's House standing amid fields.

questions.q: By the 1790s, northern states with gradual emancipation laws showed:
options: full legal equality for Black residents
the end of slavery across the nation
a nationwide ban on the slave trade
a growing regional divide over slavery
questions.explain: Northern states began ending slavery gradually while slavery grew in the South, creating a regional divide that would deepen in the decades ahead.

questions.q: Free Black communities in northern cities in the 1790s typically:
options: served as members of the House and Senate
formed churches, schools, and aid societies
voted freely in every one of the northern states
owned large farms in the western territories
questions.explain: Religious and community institutions provided support amid discrimination.

questions.q: The First Amendment's Establishment Clause means that Congress cannot:
options: establish an official national religion
levy taxes on goods imported from abroad
regulate trade among the several states
print paper money for the government
questions.explain: Together with the Free Exercise Clause, it protects religious liberty.

questions.q: Thomas Jefferson's phrase about "a wall of separation between church and state" was written in a letter to:
options: the Quakers of Philadelphia
the Pennsylvania Assembly
the Danbury Baptists
the Anglican bishops
questions.explain: Jefferson's 1802 letter interpreted the First Amendment as separating government from religious institutions.

questions.q: In 1785 James Madison's Memorial and Remonstrance helped defeat a Virginia plan to tax people for church support. Which law then passed in 1786?
options: The Bill of Rights as proposed in 1789
The Constitution as drafted at Philadelphia
The Northwest Ordinance of the Confederation
The Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom
questions.explain: Madison's Memorial and Remonstrance helped defeat a bill taxing Virginians to support Christian teachers; Jefferson's Statute for Religious Freedom then passed in 1786.

questions.q: The disestablishment of churches in several states after the Revolution reflected:
options: fear of Catholic immigration into the new nation
a widespread rejection of all organized religion
Enlightenment ideas and the growth of religious diversity
a sharp decline in membership in Protestant churches
questions.explain: The end of tax support for churches helped denominations compete for members.

questions.q: Which religious movement beginning around 1790s-1800 stressed personal conversion and emotional revivals?
options: The Second Great Awakening
The First Great Awakening
The Reformation
The Enlightenment
questions.explain: It spread through camp meetings and shaped later reform movements.

questions.q: In the late 1700s, the growth of Baptist and Methodist churches was fueled by:
options: large government grants to the dissenting churches
itinerant preachers who appealed to ordinary people
the support of the Church of England hierarchy
royal appointments of ministers to rural parishes
questions.explain: Evangelical preachers rejected formal hierarchy and drew crowds in the backcountry.

questions.q: Thomas Paine's The Age of Reason (1794) was controversial because it:
options: supported the Alien Act as a wartime measure
criticized organized Christianity and the Bible
opposed the French Revolution in an open letter
defended the monarchy against republican critics
questions.explain: Paine's deism alienated many Americans who had admired Common Sense.

questions.q: The African Methodist Episcopal Church, founded by Richard Allen, grew out of:
options: an act of Congress that funded Black congregations
a British missionary society's work in the city
a southern plantation chapel for enslaved worshippers
Black Philadelphians resisting church segregation
questions.explain: Allen and other Black worshippers left St. George's Methodist Church after trustees pulled Absalom Jones and William White from their knees during prayer.

questions.q: Which Native American religious leader of the late 1790s urged Seneca people to avoid alcohol and preserve their culture?
options: Handsome Lake
Black Hawk
Tecumseh
Pontiac
questions.explain: Handsome Lake's teachings, called the Code, spread among Haudenosaunee communities after 1799.

questions.q: The opening line of Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, "Four score and seven years ago," looks back to:
options: 1791, when the Bill of Rights was adopted
1789, when Washington took office
1776, when the Declaration was adopted
1787, when the Constitution was written
questions.explain: Lincoln subtracted eighty-seven years from 1863 to point to the Declaration's claim that all men are created equal.

questions.q: In his 1963 "I Have a Dream" speech, Martin Luther King Jr. described the Declaration and the Constitution as:
options: laws that had already ended segregation across the South
outdated papers that had little meaning for citizens in 1963
ideas copied from British law with little originality
a promissory note promising unalienable rights to all Americans
questions.explain: King argued that the founding documents contained a promise that the nation had not yet kept for Black Americans.

questions.q: Franklin D. Roosevelt's Four Freedoms speech in 1941, quoted at the FDR Memorial, built on ideas from the founding era by emphasizing:
options: protecting basic freedoms at home and abroad
isolation from world affairs and foreign conflicts
a return to hereditary rule as a model of order
the elimination of the president's war powers
questions.explain: FDR connected American ideals of liberty to global struggles.

questions.q: Jefferson's 1774 pamphlet A Summary View of the Rights of British America argued that:
options: the colonists ought to be given their own separate monarch
Parliament had no legitimate authority to make laws for the colonies
the colonies should pay taxes to Parliament in return for seats
the king had no right to veto colonial courts' decisions
questions.explain: Jefferson contended that colonists were tied to the Crown but not to Parliament, an argument that raised his profile before 1776.

questions.q: In Philadelphia in June 1776, Jefferson wrote the first draft of the Declaration while living in:
options: a tent near the Continental Army camp
rented rooms in a house on Market Street
the Pennsylvania State House cellar
Carpenters' Hall near the river docks
questions.explain: He worked in a second-floor parlor of a rented house owned by bricklayer Jacob Graff, using a portable writing desk he had designed.

questions.q: Jefferson once reported that Congress edited his draft of the Declaration heavily, which most directly suggests that the final text:
options: reflected the views of many delegates, not only its main author
was approved by Congress without any changes to Jefferson's text
was entirely replaced by a new draft written by Adams
was written in equal parts by a committee of ten
questions.explain: Congress cut roughly a fifth to a quarter of Jefferson's draft, depending on the count, including the passage on the slave trade, and made other changes.

questions.q: In 1779-1781 Jefferson served as governor of which state during the Revolution?
options: North Carolina
Pennsylvania
Virginia
Maryland
questions.explain: Jefferson moved Virginia's capital from Williamsburg to Richmond and faced British raids late in his term.

questions.q: Between 1785 and 1789, Thomas Jefferson served the United States as:
options: governor of Virginia
commissioner in London
ambassador to Spain
minister to France
questions.explain: Jefferson succeeded Franklin in Paris and witnessed the early events of the French Revolution.

questions.q: Jefferson served in Washington's first cabinet as:
options: Attorney General
Secretary of War
Secretary of the Treasury
Secretary of State
questions.explain: He disagreed sharply with Hamilton on finance and foreign policy and resigned at the end of 1793.

questions.q: Jefferson's 1784 plan for the western lands included a ban on slavery there after 1800. What happened to that clause in Congress?
options: The Supreme Court struck it down as unconstitutional
It fell one state short of the votes needed and was dropped
Washington vetoed it as president
It passed and took effect in 1800
questions.explain: Jefferson wrote that the clause was lost by a single vote; the 1784 ordinance passed without it, and the 1787 Northwest Ordinance later banned slavery north of the Ohio River.

questions.q: Jefferson's Notes on the State of Virginia (1785) was written in response to questions from a French diplomat and included:
options: a proposal for dividing the Northwest Territory into new states
detailed battle plans used in the southern campaign of 1781
a survey of Virginia's land and society, including his views on slavery
a complete list of the signers of the Declaration of Independence
questions.explain: The book, the only full-length book Jefferson published during his lifetime, mixed science with political commentary that included racial theories now seen as unfounded.

questions.q: Jefferson modeled the Virginia State House (Capitol) in Richmond on a Roman temple called the:
options: Maison Carree in Nimes, France
Parthenon in Athens, Greece
Temple of Vesta in Tivoli, Italy
Pantheon in Rome, Italy
questions.explain: Jefferson, who admired classical architecture, helped bring Roman-style design to American public buildings.

questions.q: Jefferson's idea of a nation of independent small farmers, which he thought would protect liberty, is often called:
options: mercantilism
agrarianism
industrialism
feudalism
questions.explain: Jefferson distrusted large cities and manufacturing, and believed that landowning farmers made the best citizens of a republic.

questions.q: In his 1791 opinion on the constitutionality of the Bank of the United States, Jefferson argued that:
options: only the president could lawfully create such a bank
the bank was needed to carry out Congress's war power
a bank was not among the powers listed in the Constitution
a bank could be created if Virginia's assembly approved
questions.explain: He insisted that "necessary" meant indispensable, a strict reading Hamilton rejected.

questions.q: Jefferson's first inauguration on March 4, 1801, took place in:
options: the Senate chamber of the Capitol
Independence Hall in Philadelphia
the White House State Dining Room
Federal Hall in New York
questions.explain: Jefferson was the first president inaugurated in Washington, D.C., and he walked from his boardinghouse to the Capitol.

questions.q: In his first inaugural address, Jefferson repeated Washington's advice about avoiding foreign entanglements by calling for:
options: commerce with Britain alone and no trade with any other nation
strict isolation from all trade and diplomacy with other powers
close military ties with France as a reward for its wartime help
friendship with all nations, entangling alliances with none
questions.explain: The phrase became an enduring statement of early American foreign policy.

questions.q: In 1800 Spain secretly agreed to return Louisiana to France, an event that later led Jefferson to:
options: ally with Britain against the French in Louisiana
declare war on Spain to protect the Mississippi trade
send an army to occupy Florida and the Gulf coast
try to buy New Orleans and then all of Louisiana
questions.explain: Jefferson feared French control of the mouth of the Mississippi, which led to the Louisiana Purchase in 1803.

questions.q: Jefferson's library, which he sold to Congress in 1815 to rebuild the collection, reflected his interest in:
options: military manuals and histories of European campaigns
legal treatises and the statutes of Virginia almost exclusively
a broad range of subjects, including law, science, and languages
sermons and devotional writings of the Anglican church
questions.explain: About 6,500 volumes formed the base of a new Library of Congress after the British burned the Capitol.

questions.q: Jefferson designed his home, Monticello, in which state?
options: North Carolina
Virginia
Pennsylvania
Maryland
questions.explain: Monticello, near Charlottesville, was built and rebuilt over decades by enslaved and free workers.

questions.q: Jefferson's home at Monticello was a working plantation sustained by:
options: the labor of hundreds of enslaved people over his lifetime
paid tenant farmers who rented plots from Jefferson
state prisoners sentenced to labor on private estates
conscripted soldiers assigned by the Virginia militia
questions.explain: Jefferson held over six hundred people in bondage during his lifetime, a fact that complicates his writings on liberty.

questions.q: Which statement best describes how Jefferson's Notes on the State of Virginia reveals tension in his thinking about slavery?
options: He praised slavery as a positive good for both races
He ignored slavery entirely and wrote only of geography
He demanded immediate abolition and freed his own slaves
He called slavery a danger yet did little to end it
questions.explain: Jefferson wrote that he trembled for his country when he reflected that God is just, yet he enslaved over 600 people in his lifetime and freed only seven.

questions.q: Jefferson's Bill for Establishing Religious Freedom said that forcing people to support religion was:
options: tyrannical, and civil rights do not depend on belief
required by the teachings of most Christian churches
a necessary tool for keeping social order in Virginia
acceptable so long as a majority of voters approved of it
questions.explain: The statute declared that civil rights do not depend on religious opinions.

questions.q: Which Jefferson ally from Virginia helped him lead the early Democratic-Republican opposition in Congress?
options: John Marshall
Patrick Henry
James Madison
George Mason
questions.explain: Madison and Jefferson worked together against Hamilton's financial program and Federalist foreign policy.

questions.q: John Adams and Thomas Jefferson were both members of which body in 1776?
options: The Stamp Act Congress
The Constitutional Convention
The Second Continental Congress
The First Congress
questions.explain: Adams and Jefferson both served in the Second Continental Congress in 1776 and signed the Declaration. Both later became president and died on the same day, July 4, 1826.

questions.q: In 1793, Washington asked the Supreme Court for advice on neutrality questions, but the justices:
options: declined, citing the separation of the branches
referred the question to Congress for a decision
agreed to review every law the president proposed
sent a detailed legal ruling to Washington at once
questions.explain: The refusal set a precedent that federal courts decide actual cases, not hypothetical questions.

questions.q: Ware v. Hylton (1796) reinforced the idea that:
options: only Congress has the power to cancel treaties
national treaties outrank conflicting state laws
state laws outrank treaties when passed afterward
treaties need approval by every state to be valid
questions.explain: The case, involving prewar British debts, applied the Supremacy Clause.

questions.q: John Marshall, who would shape the Court for decades, was appointed Chief Justice by:
options: Thomas Jefferson
George Washington
James Madison
John Adams
questions.explain: Adams nominated Marshall in January 1801, just before leaving office.

questions.q: Before Marshall, the Chief Justice from 1796 to 1800 was:
options: John Rutledge
John Jay
William Cushing
Oliver Ellsworth
questions.explain: Ellsworth, a Connecticut Federalist, helped write the Judiciary Act of 1789.

questions.q: Under Article III, federal judges serve:
options: for renewable four-year terms set by Congress
until the president chooses to remove them
during good behavior, effectively for life
for six-year terms with staggered elections
questions.explain: Life tenure was intended to protect judges from political pressure.

questions.q: The Supreme Court first met in February 1790 in:
options: New York City
Washington
Richmond
Philadelphia
questions.explain: The Supreme Court first met in New York City in February 1790, when New York was the capital. Chief Justice John Jay presided.

questions.q: Calder v. Bull (1798) is known for the Court:
options: striking down the Sedition Act as unconstitutional
holding that ex post facto limits cover only crimes
ruling slavery unlawful in the Northwest Territory
creating the national bank as a federal agency
questions.explain: The case was important in early debates over judges' power to limit legislatures.

questions.q: The Constitution itself does not clearly state that courts may strike down laws, but the idea of judicial review was supported in:
options: the Treaty of Paris
the Judiciary Act
Federalist No. 78
the Bill of Rights
questions.explain: Hamilton argued that courts must declare void acts contrary to the Constitution.

questions.q: Which early justice, a signer of the Declaration and Constitution, was also a leading legal thinker of the founding era?
options: John Marshall
John Rutledge
Samuel Chase
James Wilson
questions.explain: Wilson of Pennsylvania argued for popular sovereignty and served on the first Court.

questions.q: Justice Samuel Chase, impeached in 1804, had been a signer of the Declaration and:
options: a Loyalist who left the country during the war
a Federalist known for harsh Sedition Act rulings
a Democratic-Republican leader in the Senate
a delegate to the Constitutional Convention in 1787
questions.explain: The House impeached him in 1804, but the Senate acquitted him in 1805.

questions.q: Which Supreme Court case from the 1790s grew from a suit against Georgia by a South Carolina citizen?
options: Calder v. Bull
Chisholm v. Georgia
Ware v. Hylton
Hylton v. United States
questions.explain: Alexander Chisholm, executor for a South Carolina merchant, sued to collect on a wartime debt.

questions.q: Federal courts can hear cases involving:
options: the Constitution, federal laws, and treaties
only local disputes within a single county
only criminal cases brought by the states
only foreign wars declared by Congress
questions.explain: Article III extends judicial power to such cases, along with disputes between states.

questions.q: Before the Constitution, the Continental Congress printed paper money called "Continentals," which:
options: held its value because it was backed by gold reserves
was accepted at full value in the ports of Europe
lost nearly all value, hence "not worth a Continental"
became the stable foundation of the nation's dollar
questions.explain: Without taxing power, Congress printed money that rapidly depreciated.

questions.q: Robert Morris, Superintendent of Finance during the Revolution, helped fund the war by:
options: levying direct taxes on property in the states
seizing Loyalist property for resale to patriots
selling western land claims to foreign investors
securing loans and founding the Bank of North America
questions.explain: The bank was the first chartered in the United States and helped stabilize government finances.

questions.q: Alexander Hamilton began his service with George Washington during the Revolution as:
options: an aide-de-camp and trusted staff officer
a Loyalist spy inside the British headquarters
a naval captain commanding a privateer
a quartermaster in charge of army supplies
questions.explain: Hamilton served on Washington's staff for several years and commanded a battalion at Yorktown.

questions.q: Hamilton led an assault on a British fortification at Yorktown known as:
options: Fort Washington
Bunker Hill
Redoubt 10
Fort Ticonderoga
questions.explain: On October 14, 1781, Hamilton led the night assault that captured Redoubt 10 while French troops took Redoubt 9. Cornwallis surrendered five days later.

questions.q: The United States Revenue Marine (later the Coast Guard) was created in 1790 to:
options: carry mail between the major seaports
transport troops to the western frontier
fight pirates along the Pacific coast
enforce customs laws and prevent smuggling
questions.explain: Hamilton proposed a fleet of revenue cutters to collect import duties at American ports.

questions.q: The first U.S. Mint in Philadelphia began producing coins in 1792, and its first director was:
options: Robert Morris
David Rittenhouse
Benjamin Rush
Tench Coxe
questions.explain: David Rittenhouse, a noted astronomer and instrument maker, was the first director of the U.S. Mint, founded in Philadelphia in 1792.

questions.q: The United States' first federal source of revenue was:
options: income taxes
property taxes
land sales
tariffs on imports
questions.explain: Duties on imported goods provided most federal income in the early republic.

questions.q: Hamilton resigned from the Treasury in 1795, but he remained influential through:
options: his seat in the United States Senate from New York
advice to Washington and Federalist leadership
his role as leader of the Democratic-Republicans
his service as chief justice of the Supreme Court
questions.explain: He helped draft Washington's Farewell Address and continued to shape Federalist policy.

questions.q: Which argument did Hamilton make for paying the national debt at face value?
options: It would remove the need for a national bank
It would help small farmers more than investors
Full payment would prove the government reliable
It would lower taxes for most citizens right away
questions.explain: Hamilton reasoned that credit was essential to national strength.

questions.q: Critics of Hamilton's funding plan, such as Madison, worried that it would:
options: reward speculators who had bought bonds at a discount
end the tariff that raised revenue for the government
ruin the merchants who traded in the northern ports
destroy the borrowing power of the states
questions.explain: Madison proposed paying original holders in part, but Congress rejected the idea.

questions.q: The Senate held its early sessions behind closed doors until:
options: 1826, when Jefferson and Adams died
1794-1795, when it opened its galleries
1812, when the war with Britain began
1800, when the government moved to Washington
questions.explain: The Senate opened its doors in 1795, six years after the House had allowed the public in.

questions.q: Which senator, a member of the Senate since 1796, was expelled in 1797 for conspiring to help Britain take Spanish territory?
options: Rufus King
Aaron Burr
Robert Morris
William Blount
questions.explain: Blount was expelled in 1797 and the House impeached him, but the Senate dismissed the case.

questions.q: William Blount, expelled from the Senate in 1797, represented which state?
options: Virginia
New York
Tennessee
Pennsylvania
questions.explain: He was one of the first two senators from Tennessee, the sixteenth state.

questions.q: The Senate and House together are called:
options: Congress
the Electoral College
the Assembly
the Cabinet
questions.explain: Article I vests all legislative powers in a bicameral Congress.

questions.q: The Constitution requires a national census every ten years to:
options: apportion seats in the House of Representatives
select the senators from each of the states
name the next president of the United States
set the number of justices on the Supreme Court
questions.explain: The first census took place in 1790 and counted about 3.9 million people.

questions.q: About what share of the people counted in the first census of 1790 were enslaved?
options: About one in twenty
About one in three
About half
About one in six
questions.explain: More than 690,000 people were held in slavery in 1790, mostly in the South.

questions.q: Washington's first veto, in 1792, rejected a bill about:
options: a tariff on imported manufactured goods
how to apportion seats in the House
a treaty with Great Britain over the forts
the charter of the Bank of the United States
questions.explain: Washington vetoed the first apportionment bill on constitutional grounds, and Congress passed a new one.

questions.q: How many votes of each house are needed to override a presidential veto?
options: Two-thirds
Three-fourths
A simple majority
Unanimity
questions.explain: The Constitution requires a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate to override a veto. The high bar means most vetoes stand.

questions.q: Congress passed the first copyright and patent laws in 1790 under the power to:
options: raise and support armies in time of war
regulate commerce among the several states
punish counterfeiting of the national coin
promote the progress of science and useful arts
questions.explain: Article I gave Congress the power to protect authors and inventors for limited times.

questions.q: The Post Office Act of 1792 helped:
options: pay for the army through a surplus of postal revenue
spread news by letting newspapers be mailed at low rates
protect the seacoast by hiring ships to carry the mail
shorten travel time on the road between the major cities
questions.explain: Cheap postal rates for newspapers helped build a national political conversation.

questions.q: The Lancaster Turnpike, completed in 1795, was notable as:
options: the first steam railroad line in the United States
a long canal linking Philadelphia and New York harbor
one of the first long paved toll roads in the nation
a military supply road built to serve Wayne's army in Ohio
questions.explain: The turnpike linked Philadelphia and Lancaster, Pennsylvania, and became a model for private road building.

questions.q: The Confederation Congress approved the Treaty of Paris in January 1784 in:
options: Annapolis, Maryland
Boston, Massachusetts
Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
New York, New York
questions.explain: Congress met in the Maryland State House in Annapolis, where Washington had resigned his commission the month before.

questions.q: In June 1783, Congress left Philadelphia after soldiers protested unpaid wages, which helped lead the framers to:
options: ban all soldiers from entering the capital city at any time
limit Congress to meeting only six months a year
give Congress control over its own federal district
move the national capital to a northern seaport
questions.explain: The mutiny showed the danger of depending on a state to protect Congress, a lesson written into the Constitution.

questions.q: The Confederation Congress met in several cities, including:
options: Williamsburg, Charleston, Savannah, and Newport
Washington, Georgetown, Alexandria, and Richmond
Boston, Hartford, Baltimore, Richmond, and Savannah
Philadelphia, Princeton, Annapolis, Trenton, and New York
questions.explain: The lack of a permanent capital added to the sense that the government was weak.

questions.q: The Constitution forbids Congress from taxing exports, which most directly protected:
options: New England manufacturers who exported goods
southern states that sold crops abroad
the state militias of the northern states
western land speculators in Kentucky
questions.explain: The ban was part of a bargain with delegates from the South.

questions.q: Which clause lets Congress decide whether the nation goes to war?
options: The Treaty Clause in Article II
The power to declare war in Article I
The Supremacy Clause of Article VI
The Commander in Chief Clause in Article II
questions.explain: The framers gave the power to declare war to Congress, not the president.

questions.q: The Constitution makes the president:
options: commander in chief of the army and navy
head of the Supreme Court and lower courts
secretary of war for the entire nation
chief officer of both houses of Congress
questions.explain: While Congress declares war and funds the military, the president commands it.

questions.q: The 1789 First Congress also created the first executive departments, which were:
options: Navy, Justice, and Post
Energy, Defense, and Education
Interior, Labor, and Commerce
State, Treasury, and War
questions.explain: These departments, along with the Attorney General, formed Washington's cabinet.

questions.q: The Continental Army was created by:
options: Parliament through an act passed in 1774
the Constitutional Convention in 1787
the Second Continental Congress in June 1775
the Articles of Confederation in 1781
questions.explain: Congress adopted the New England militia around Boston as a continental force.

questions.q: The Marine Corps traces its origin to November 1775, when the Continental Congress authorized:
options: a regiment of sharpshooters for the southern army
a single company of cavalry for Washington's staff
two battalions of marines for service on ships
a coastal militia for the defense of the ports
questions.explain: The marines were first recruited in Philadelphia, including at Tun Tavern according to tradition.

questions.q: John Paul Jones is remembered for the line "I have not yet begun to fight" during a battle in:
options: 1781 against ships blockading Yorktown
1776 against the British ship Glasgow
1798 against French privateers off Haiti
1779 against the British ship Serapis
questions.explain: Jones's ship Bonhomme Richard won the battle despite heavy damage.

questions.q: In 1794 Congress authorized the first U.S. Navy frigates, in part to:
options: defend merchant ships from Barbary pirates
attack French privateers in the Caribbean Sea
patrol the Great Lakes against British ships
blockade British ports on the English Channel
questions.explain: The Naval Act led to the construction of ships such as the USS Constitution, launched in 1797.

questions.q: Washington's Legion of the United States, formed in 1792, was designed to:
options: replace the state militias with a national draft
build a better trained army for frontier warfare
defend the Atlantic coast from a British landing
protect the western rivers from Spanish raids
questions.explain: The reorganization followed St. Clair's defeat and led to Wayne's victory at Fallen Timbers.

questions.q: The Militia Act of 1792 required that:
options: all free men over sixteen join the regular army
only volunteers who signed for years could serve
free white men aged 18 to 45 enroll in militias
each state raise a regular army of 5,000 men
questions.explain: Local militia remained central to defense, with states providing the manpower.

questions.q: Which American general's treason in 1780 shocked the nation when he plotted to turn over West Point to the British?
options: Anthony Wayne
Benedict Arnold
Horatio Gates
Charles Lee
questions.explain: Arnold's plot was uncovered when British spy John Andre was captured.

questions.q: The southern campaign of 1780-1781 included an American victory at Cowpens under:
options: Daniel Morgan
Horatio Gates
Benjamin Lincoln
Anthony Wayne
questions.explain: Morgan's tactics defeated Banastre Tarleton and weakened Cornwallis' army.

questions.q: The largest American surrender of the Revolutionary War occurred in 1780 at:
options: Camden, South Carolina
Savannah, Georgia
Yorktown, Virginia
Charleston, South Carolina
questions.explain: General Benjamin Lincoln surrendered about 5,000 troops to the British.

questions.q: The 1780 patriot victory at Kings Mountain was won largely by:
options: French regulars sent from Rochambeau's army
ships of the Continental Navy on the coast
Hessian mercenaries hired by the British
frontier militia, who defeated a Loyalist force
questions.explain: The battle turned momentum in the Carolinas toward the Patriots.

questions.q: General Nathanael Greene is best known for:
options: commanding the American forces at the Battle of Saratoga
defending Boston during the siege of 1775-76
leading the southern campaign that wore down Cornwallis
negotiating the French alliance with Louis XVI
questions.explain: Greene avoided decisive defeat and forced the British out of most of the Carolinas and Georgia.

questions.q: Which Polish engineer helped design fortifications at Saratoga and West Point?
options: Thaddeus Kosciuszko
Casimir Pulaski
Marquis de Lafayette
Baron de Kalb
questions.explain: Kosciuszko's defenses at Saratoga helped bring the victory that led to the French alliance.

questions.q: George Washington Parke Custis, who built Arlington House, was:
options: a cousin of George Washington from Westmoreland
Washington's step-grandson, raised at Mount Vernon
George Washington's son by an earlier marriage
George Washington's nephew from Fredericksburg
questions.explain: Custis built the house as a memorial to Washington and filled it with relics.

questions.q: Arlington House was designed to be a living memorial to:
options: Thomas Jefferson
Benjamin Franklin
John Adams
George Washington
questions.explain: Custis displayed Washington's belongings there, and the house later became linked to Robert E. Lee.

questions.q: Why was George Washington's choice to give up power and return to Mount Vernon in 1783 widely praised?
options: Victors often kept power, but Washington chose to retire
He wanted to travel across Europe after the war
He had no soldiers left to command after the peace
He feared the new government would arrest him
questions.explain: King George III reportedly said that if Washington gave up power he would be the greatest man in the world.

questions.q: Joseph Brant, a Mohawk leader, is best known for:
