options: writing speeches for the Continental Congress
serving as a scout and aide on Washington's staff
leading Native and Loyalist forces on Britain's side
leading the Western Confederacy at Fallen Timbers
questions.explain: Brant fought to protect Haudenosaunee lands from American settlement.

questions.q: The Treaty of Fort Stanwix (1784) forced the Haudenosaunee to:
options: join the United States as full citizens at once
give up their weapons and swear a loyalty oath
move permanently to Canada under British protection
give up claims to the Ohio Country and western lands
questions.explain: The treaty was signed under pressure after the Revolution, and many Native leaders did not accept it.

questions.q: The Oneida and Tuscarora nations, unlike most Haudenosaunee, during the Revolution:
options: fought with the British
left for the Ohio country
sided with the American cause
remained entirely neutral
questions.explain: Oneida supply and scouts aided the Americans at Oriskany and Valley Forge.

questions.q: The Treaty of Canandaigua (1794) between the United States and the Haudenosaunee:
options: created a new state reserved for the Haudenosaunee
confirmed Haudenosaunee lands in New York and is still honored
ended the Haudenosaunee Confederacy as a political nation
granted the Haudenosaunee full U.S. citizenship
questions.explain: The treaty is commemorated each year with a cloth presented at the signing.

questions.q: Cherokee leader Dragging Canoe led a faction in the Revolution that:
options: fought settlers who were moving onto Cherokee land
moved west across the Mississippi to avoid the war
negotiated peace with Virginia in the first year
supported the Continental Army against the British
questions.explain: His group, the Chickamauga, kept fighting after other Cherokee leaders made peace.

questions.q: Which 1790 law gave the federal government control over the sale of Native lands?
options: The Trade and Intercourse Act
The Indian Removal Act of 1830
The Land Ordinance of 1785
The Dawes Severalty Act of 1887
questions.explain: The law said that only the federal government could buy land from Native nations, but enforcement was weak.

questions.q: Which cabinet officer carried out much of Washington's policy toward Native nations?
options: Alexander Hamilton
Henry Knox
Thomas Jefferson
Edmund Randolph
questions.explain: As Secretary of War, Knox favored negotiation and encouraged Native adoption of farming.

questions.q: The Northwest Indian War of 1785-1795 was fought over:
options: the Great Lakes fisheries
Florida
control of the Ohio Country
the Mississippi River
questions.explain: The war ended with Wayne's victory and the Treaty of Greenville.

questions.q: In 1782, militiamen killed ninety-six peaceful Christian Delaware (Lenape) at Gnadenhutten in:
options: Virginia
Georgia
New York
Ohio country
questions.explain: The massacre was among the worst atrocities against Native people during the Revolution.

questions.q: In Dunmore's War of 1774, Virginia's royal governor:
options: fought the Haudenosaunee to open western New York
fought the Cherokee to protect the Carolina coast
fought the Shawnee to open Ohio Valley land
allied with Spain to secure the Mississippi
questions.explain: The Shawnee were forced to cede claims south of the Ohio River.

questions.q: Most Native nations that took sides in the Revolution chose Britain because:
options: they saw the Crown as a limit on settlement
they feared the French would return to the region
they respected the king as a ruler of all peoples
they hoped to live under British rule in London
questions.explain: Many Native leaders saw the Proclamation of 1763 and British restraints as better protection than the colonists.

questions.q: When the Constitution refers to Native nations, it:
options: grants them seats in the House of Representatives
lets Congress regulate commerce with the Indian tribes
leaves all dealings with Native nations to the states
makes each Native nation a state in the Union
questions.explain: The Commerce Clause names Indian tribes alongside foreign nations and the states.

questions.q: The Treaty of Paris of 1783 did not mention Native nations, and so:
options: they became U.S. citizens by the terms of the treaty
they willingly gave up their claims to western lands
they asked Britain to protect them against the states
many of them rejected U.S. claims to their lands
questions.explain: Native leaders argued that Britain could not give away land it did not own.

questions.q: In 1796, Ona Judge escaped from the President's House in Philadelphia and fled to:
options: New Hampshire
Massachusetts
Ohio
Canada
questions.explain: Judge, enslaved by Martha Washington, escaped to Portsmouth, where Washington's agents tried to retrieve her.

questions.q: Washington rotated enslaved people out of Pennsylvania every six months in the 1790s to:
options: follow a federal law that required the practice
save money on the cost of housing them in the city
protect their health from yellow fever in the city
avoid Pennsylvania's gradual abolition law
questions.explain: Pennsylvania law freed enslaved people held in the state beyond six months, so he sent people out and back.

questions.q: James Armistead, an enslaved Virginian, contributed at Yorktown by serving as:
options: a ship's pilot on the French fleet at Yorktown
a surgeon in a Virginia militia hospital camp
a spy who gave Lafayette British information
a drummer in the Virginia militia regiment
questions.explain: James Armistead posed as a servant in British camps and passed information to Lafayette before Yorktown. After winning his freedom, he took the name James Armistead Lafayette.

questions.q: Many Black Loyalists who left with the British after the war went to:
options: only the British islands of the Caribbean
Nova Scotia, Britain, and later Sierra Leone
free Black towns across the northern states
the Ohio country and the Northwest Territory
questions.explain: The British recorded those evacuated from New York in the Book of Negroes.

questions.q: Elizabeth Freeman (Mum Bett) won her freedom in 1781 by:
options: buying her freedom with money saved from her labor
escaping to British lines during the siege of Boston
petitioning the king in London for her release
suing in a Massachusetts court over its constitution
questions.explain: Her case helped show that slavery conflicted with the constitution's declaration of freedom.

questions.q: Prince Hall, a free Black leader in Boston, is notable for founding which institution during the Revolutionary era?
options: African Lodge, a Black Masonic lodge
A Black regiment
A school for girls
An antislavery newspaper
questions.explain: Hall won a charter for African Lodge from the Grand Lodge of England in 1784, though it reached Boston only in 1787; he also petitioned Massachusetts against slavery.

questions.q: Olaudah Equiano's 1789 autobiography became important because it:
options: explained how the new Constitution protected property
described the slave trade firsthand, aiding abolitionism
described the military campaigns of the American Revolution
defended slavery as a necessary part of the Atlantic economy
questions.explain: The memoir was widely read and helped build antislavery sentiment.

questions.q: Virginia's 1782 law on manumission:
options: freed all children born to enslaved mothers
abolished slavery throughout the state of Virginia
made it easier for owners to free enslaved people
banned all private freeing of enslaved people
questions.explain: Many enslaved people were freed in the following years, though Virginia later tightened its rules, requiring freed people to leave the state.

questions.q: In 1797, Hercules, a chef enslaved by Washington, escaped from:
options: Mount Vernon
New York
Williamsburg
Richmond
questions.explain: Hercules fled on Washington's birthday and was never recaptured.

questions.q: Peter Salem is remembered for:
options: commanding a privateer out of Newport harbor in 1777
signing the Declaration as a Massachusetts delegate
writing poetry that won praise in London and Boston
serving in the militia at Lexington and Bunker Hill
questions.explain: Salem, once enslaved, earned his freedom by serving in the army.

questions.q: The Pennsylvania Abolition Society, with Benjamin Franklin as an officer, worked to:
options: defend the rights of slaveholders in court
end slavery and protect free Black people
open a school for the children of settlers
found a colony for freed people in Africa
questions.explain: The Pennsylvania Abolition Society worked to end slavery and to protect free Black people from being kidnapped into slavery. Franklin became its president in 1787.

questions.q: The Constitution does not use the word "slavery," but it protects slavery through the Fugitive Slave Clause, the Slave Trade Clause, and:
options: the Emoluments Clause
the Preamble
the Three-Fifths Clause
the Commerce Clause alone
questions.explain: The three-fifths rule strengthened the political power of slave states.

questions.q: Which British monarch ruled during the American Revolution and was the target of the Declaration's list of grievances?
options: King Charles II
King William III
King George II
King George III
questions.explain: George III reigned from 1760 to 1820 and was the Declaration's main target.

questions.q: Paul Revere is best remembered for his April 1775 ride to:
options: rally the Sons of Liberty to dump tea in the harbor
deliver the Olive Branch Petition to King George
warn the militia that British troops were on the march
carry the Declaration of Independence to Georgia
questions.explain: Revere, William Dawes, and Samuel Prescott spread the alarm before Lexington and Concord.

questions.q: In May 1775, Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys captured which fort, gaining cannon for the patriot army?
options: Fort Sumter
Fort Ticonderoga
Fort Duquesne
Fort McHenry
questions.explain: The captured artillery was later moved to Boston by Henry Knox.

questions.q: The Quartering Act of 1765 required colonists to:
options: provide housing and supplies for British soldiers
buy all of their tea from a single company
stay east of the Appalachian crest in the future
pay a duty on every newspaper and legal paper
questions.explain: The Quartering Act was one of the measures colonists resented as part of imperial reform.

questions.q: In 1761, lawyer James Otis argued against writs of assistance, which allowed customs officers to:
options: seize ships and cargoes without a trial in court
levy taxes on goods without a vote in assembly
search homes and warehouses without specific warrants
force sailors to serve on Royal Navy warships
questions.explain: Otis's argument is often seen as a forerunner of Fourth Amendment ideas.

questions.q: Which Virginia delegate declared "Give me liberty, or give me death!" in a March 1775 speech?
options: Patrick Henry
George Mason
Richard Henry Lee
Thomas Jefferson
questions.explain: Henry urged Virginia to arm its militia in March 1775; the famous wording comes from an account published decades later.

questions.q: In The American Crisis (1776), Thomas Paine wrote "These are the times that try men's souls" to encourage:
options: merchants who opposed the boycotts of British goods
Loyalists who were considering a return to Britain
delegates debating the new Constitution in Philadelphia
discouraged soldiers during the retreat across New Jersey
questions.explain: Washington had the essay read to his troops before the crossing of the Delaware.

questions.q: The Hessians, who fought for Britain, were:
options: German soldiers hired by the British government
Native allies recruited from the Ohio country
Loyalist militia raised in New York and Georgia
French volunteers serving under British officers
questions.explain: Britain hired thousands of troops from German states such as Hesse-Kassel.

questions.q: In September 1777 the British army captured which American capital city?
options: Boston
Philadelphia
New York
Baltimore
questions.explain: Congress fled, and the British held the city until June 1778.

questions.q: A legislature with two houses is called:
options: confederal
federal
bicameral
unicameral
questions.explain: A bicameral legislature has two houses. Congress is bicameral, with a House of Representatives and a Senate.

questions.q: In the Constitution, which branch is responsible for interpreting the laws?
options: The legislative branch
The judicial branch
The Electoral College
The executive branch
questions.explain: Article III sets up the Supreme Court and lower federal courts.

questions.q: The Constitution gives the executive power to:
options: the Senate leader
the chief justice
the Speaker of the House
the president
questions.explain: Article II of the Constitution vests executive power in the president, who carries out the laws and commands the armed forces.

questions.q: How long is a presidential term under the Constitution?
options: Two years
Six years
Four years
Eight years
questions.explain: Article II sets four-year terms, and the Twenty-second Amendment later limited presidents to two elected terms.

questions.q: George Washington's home on the Potomac River in Virginia was:
options: Mount Vernon
Arlington House
Montpelier
Monticello
questions.explain: Washington lived at Mount Vernon before and after his presidency.

questions.q: Who was the third president of the United States?
options: Thomas Jefferson
John Adams
James Monroe
James Madison
questions.explain: Jefferson took office in 1801 after defeating Adams in 1800.

questions.q: Abigail Adams was known as John Adams' close adviser, and she lived in the unfinished President's House in:
questions.explain: She joined the president in November 1800 and hung laundry in the unfinished East Room.

questions.q: Which Founder is known for flying a kite in a storm to study electricity?
options: James Madison
Alexander Hamilton
Thomas Jefferson
Benjamin Franklin
questions.explain: Franklin also invented the lightning rod and bifocal glasses.

questions.q: Benjamin Franklin served the Continental Congress in 1775 as the first:
options: Treasury Secretary
Postmaster General
Chief Justice
Attorney General
questions.explain: He had run colonial post offices under the Crown and organized a postal system for Congress.

questions.q: The Second Continental Congress adopted the first national flag in 1777, which featured:
options: fifty stars and thirteen stripes
a rattlesnake and a pine tree
a red cross on white
thirteen stars and thirteen stripes
questions.explain: The Flag Act of June 14, 1777, called for thirteen alternating red and white stripes and thirteen white stars on a blue field, one for each state.

questions.q: The Liberty Bell is displayed in which city?
options: Boston
New York
Philadelphia
Williamsburg
questions.explain: The bell hung in the Pennsylvania State House, now Independence Hall.

questions.q: How many pages does the Constitution's original signed text have?
options: Four
Ten
Twelve
One
questions.explain: The four large parchment sheets are displayed at the National Archives.

questions.q: The engrossed (parchment) Declaration of Independence is generally attributed to which penman?
options: Charles Thomson
John Hancock
Timothy Matlack
Thomas Jefferson
questions.explain: Matlack, a Philadelphia clerk, is believed to have penned the engrossed copy that most delegates signed on August 2, 1776.

questions.q: The first printed copies of the Declaration, made on the night of July 4, 1776, were produced by:
options: Isaiah Thomas, a Worcester printer
John Dunlap, a Philadelphia printer
Hugh Gaine, a New York printer
William Goddard, a Baltimore printer
questions.explain: The Dunlap broadsides spread the Declaration; only about twenty-six survive.

questions.q: The Declaration was read publicly in Philadelphia for the first time on:
options: July 8, 1776
August 2, 1776
June 7, 1776
July 4, 1776
questions.explain: John Nixon read it aloud outside the State House, and Washington had it read to his troops in New York the next day.

questions.q: After hearing the Declaration read in New York in July 1776, a crowd:
options: dumped a cargo of tea into the Hudson River
marched on the British fleet in New York harbor
burned the home of a prominent Loyalist
pulled down a statue of King George III
questions.explain: After the Declaration was read in New York on July 9, 1776, a crowd pulled down a lead statue of King George III at Bowling Green. The lead was later melted into musket balls.

questions.q: In his first inaugural address, Lincoln argued that the Union was older than the Constitution, tracing its start to the:
options: Treaty of Paris of 1783
Northwest Ordinance of 1787
Judiciary Act of 1789
Continental Association of 1774
questions.explain: Lincoln said the Union was formed by the Articles of Association in 1774, then matured by the Declaration and the Articles of Confederation.

questions.q: In what way were the colonial nonimportation boycotts similar to later protests like the Montgomery bus boycott?
options: Both relied on armed force to achieve their goals quickly
Both used economic pressure to press for political change
Both were organized by royal officials in London
Both aimed to create a new independent nation
questions.explain: Refusing to buy or ride can be a powerful form of protest, as colonists learned in the 1760s.

questions.q: After the Revolution, the Church of England in America reorganized as the:
options: Lutheran Church
Presbyterian Church
Episcopal Church
Congregational Church
questions.explain: After independence, American Anglicans could no longer be tied to the British crown, so they reorganized as the Protestant Episcopal Church in 1789.

questions.q: Massachusetts continued to support the Congregational Church with public money until:
questions.explain: Several New England states kept established churches after the Revolution.

questions.q: In 1789, President Washington issued the first proclamation under the new Constitution calling for a national day of:
options: thanksgiving and prayer
independence and celebration
labor and public industry
remembrance of fallen soldiers
questions.explain: Washington proclaimed a day of thanksgiving to recognize the Constitution and the nation's blessings.

questions.q: The Potowmack Company, which Washington promoted in the 1780s, aimed to:
options: operate ferries across the river at Georgetown and Alexandria
improve river navigation to link the coast and the west
build a turnpike from Alexandria to the Ohio River
build a canal between Chesapeake and Delaware Bays
questions.explain: The company built locks and canals around falls on the river.

questions.q: In the 1790s and early 1800s, most travelers between cities such as Philadelphia and Washington used:
options: automobiles and paved highways
railroads and steam-powered ferries
subways and electric trolleys
stagecoaches, horses, and ships
questions.explain: Before railroads, travelers between cities went by stagecoach, on horseback or by ship. Unpaved roads made trips slow and uncomfortable.

questions.q: In 1798, during the Quasi-War with France, Adams called Washington out of retirement to command:
options: the provisional army as lieutenant general
the new Navy as admiral of the fleet
the Senate as its first presiding officer
the Supreme Court as its third chief justice
questions.explain: Washington accepted but asked Hamilton to carry out the work of organizing.

questions.q: The Society of the Cincinnati, formed in 1783 by Continental Army officers, took its name from:
options: a Spanish explorer of the western lands
a Roman leader who gave up power
a Greek philosopher who taught freedom
a French king who inspired the republic
questions.explain: The name honored Cincinnatus, a Roman who returned to his farm after saving Rome.

questions.q: The Society of the Cincinnati drew criticism because:
options: it admitted enslaved men to full membership
it was secretly funded by the British Crown
opponents feared a hereditary military aristocracy
it openly opposed ratification of the Constitution
questions.explain: Critics, such as Benjamin Franklin, worried that membership passed to eldest sons.

questions.q: George Washington first gained military experience as an officer in the:
options: Continental Army
Virginia militia
British navy
French army
questions.explain: Washington first served as an officer in the Virginia militia in the 1750s, gaining experience on the frontier during the French and Indian War.

questions.q: In 1755, Washington survived General Braddock's defeat near:
options: the Monongahela River in western Pennsylvania
Lake Champlain in northern New York
the Chesapeake Bay on the coast of Virginia
Boston Harbor at the start of the war
questions.explain: Braddock's army was ambushed near the Monongahela River in 1755 by French and Native forces. Washington survived, though two horses were shot from under him.

questions.q: Washington's 1783 "Circular to the States" urged Americans to support:
options: state sovereignty above any national government
a ban on political parties in all states
the creation of a monarchy to unify the thirteen states
an indissoluble union and a strong central authority
questions.explain: He warned that without a firm union, the nation's independence would be in danger.

questions.q: L'Enfant's plan for Washington, D.C., reserved a spot for an equestrian statue of Washington near the site where:
options: the Washington Monument was later built
the Supreme Court building now stands
the White House now stands on its grounds
the Capitol building now stands today
questions.explain: The Monument stands slightly southeast of L'Enfant's planned location because of marshy ground.

questions.q: The fresco on the dome of the Capitol Rotunda, completed in 1865, is called:
options: The Spirit of '76
The Signing of the Constitution
The Surrender at Yorktown
The Apotheosis of Washington
questions.explain: Constantino Brumidi painted George Washington rising to the heavens amid figures from classical mythology.

questions.q: John Trumbull's Rotunda painting of the surrender at Yorktown depicts:
options: Washington crossing the Delaware to attack Trenton
Burgoyne's surrender to General Gates at Saratoga
the surrender of Cornwallis's army to Washington's
the signing of the Treaty of Paris by commissioners
questions.explain: Trumbull painted the surrender of General Cornwallis, although Cornwallis himself did not attend.

questions.q: Which three people played major roles in the early design and construction of the Capitol?
options: James Hoban, Thomas Jefferson, and William Strickland
William Thornton, Stephen Hallet, and Benjamin Latrobe
James Madison, Thomas Jefferson, and Alexander Hamilton
Pierre L'Enfant, George Washington, and Andrew Ellicott
questions.explain: Thornton won, Hallet was involved in early work, and Latrobe later became the architect of the Capitol.

questions.q: The Mitchell Map of 1755, used in the Treaty of Paris negotiations of 1783, showed:
options: the constellations used by sailors for navigation
the Pacific coast from California to Alaska
eastern North America and its colonial boundaries
the major ocean currents of the North Atlantic
questions.explain: Negotiators relied on the map to draw the boundary of the new nation.

questions.q: The Library of Congress holds Jefferson's rough draft of the Declaration, which reveals:
options: how Congress edited his language
a plan for the Constitution
that Franklin wrote it
a poem by Jefferson
questions.explain: The document includes changes by Adams, Franklin, and others, and Jefferson's own notes.

questions.q: The Library of Congress is the nation's:
options: first federal court of appeals
first military post in the capital
first publicly funded university
oldest federal cultural institution
questions.explain: It was founded in 1800 and moved into its own building in 1897.

questions.q: The "Book of Negroes" recorded:
options: enslaved people sold in the Charleston market
Black people the British evacuated from New York
Black signers of petitions to the First Congress
Black soldiers who served in the Continental Army
questions.explain: It documents those who left the new United States with the British, many hoping for freedom.

questions.q: A treaty between the United States and a Native nation in the 1780s and 1790s was typically negotiated:
options: as local ordinances enforced by county sheriffs
by state courts acting on their own authority
as military orders issued by the commanding general
as agreements between governments, often under pressure
questions.explain: The Constitution treats treaties as supreme law, and early treaties were made nation to nation.

questions.q: The head of the Supreme Court is called the:
options: Chief Justice
Majority Leader
Speaker
Attorney General
questions.explain: The Chief Justice presides over the Court and, in the Senate, over a presidential impeachment trial.

questions.q: In a presidential impeachment trial, which official presides in the Senate?
options: The Senate leader
The Speaker
The Chief Justice
The vice president
questions.explain: The Constitution requires the Chief Justice to preside when the president is tried.

questions.q: The presiding officer of the House of Representatives is the:
options: chief justice
secretary of state
Speaker of the House
vice president
questions.explain: The Constitution says the House chooses its Speaker; the first was Frederick Muhlenberg.

questions.q: The number of representatives each state has in the House depends on its:
options: age
population
area
wealth
questions.explain: Every state gets at least one representative, and seats are reapportioned after each census.

questions.q: The Bank of the United States, created in 1791, was headquartered in:
options: Philadelphia
New York
Washington
Boston
questions.explain: The first Bank of the United States was based in Philadelphia, then the temporary capital. Congress gave it a 20-year charter.

questions.q: The "cabinet" is the group of:
options: department heads who advise the president
senators chosen from each of the states
governors who lead each of the states
justices who sit on the Supreme Court
questions.explain: The Constitution does not name a cabinet, but it grew from Washington's practice.

questions.q: The Barbary pirates, who attacked American merchant ships, operated from North Africa and demanded:
options: American land for new naval bases
weapons from the American arsenals
tribute payments for safe passage
trade rights in the port of Boston
questions.explain: The United States paid tribute in the 1790s before fighting the Barbary Wars under Jefferson.

questions.q: The Second Amendment protects the right to:
options: avoid giving testimony against oneself in court
keep and bear arms, tied to a well-regulated militia
refuse to quarter soldiers in private homes
petition the government to redress grievances
questions.explain: The amendment's wording about a militia reflects the era's concerns about standing armies.

questions.q: The Seventh Amendment guarantees the right to:
options: protection from quartering
a speedy trial in criminal cases
freedom of religion
a jury trial in certain civil cases
questions.explain: Preserving civil juries was important to many Antifederalists.

questions.q: The "due process" clause in the Fifth Amendment limits:
options: the government's power to quarter troops without consent
power to deprive people of life or property unfairly
the government's power to deny a jury in civil cases
the government's power to set bail at excessive levels
questions.explain: Due process later became a major issue in constitutional law.

questions.q: In the First Amendment, "free exercise" of religion means:
options: the government may not target religious practice
only Christian churches receive legal protection
the government must choose one national church
public schools must teach a single religion
questions.explain: The Free Exercise Clause works with the Establishment Clause.

questions.q: The principle of "checks and balances" is meant to:
options: give the president the final say on every law passed
let the states control the national army in peacetime
prevent any branch of government from becoming too powerful
end regular elections for members of the House
questions.explain: Checks and balances give each branch of government ways to limit the others, such as the presidential veto and Senate approval of appointments, so no branch becomes too powerful.

questions.q: When the Senate holds a trial after an impeachment, conviction requires:
options: a simple majority
a unanimous vote
a three-fourths vote
a two-thirds vote
questions.explain: Conviction in an impeachment trial requires a two-thirds vote of senators present. The framers set this high bar to make removal from office difficult.

questions.q: Which fact about the population of the new United States in 1790 is accurate?
options: Most people lived in rural areas and worked in farming
Most people lived in large cities near the coast
Most people lived west of the Appalachian Mountains
Most people worked in factories making textiles
questions.explain: Only about 5 percent of Americans lived in towns of 2,500 or more.

questions.q: According to the 1790 census, the largest city in the United States was:
options: Baltimore
New York
Boston
Philadelphia
questions.explain: New York had about 33,000 people in 1790, ahead of Philadelphia, Boston, and Baltimore.

questions.q: When the Declaration of Independence calls certain truths "self-evident," it means that they are:
options: proved by the rulings of English courts
written into the laws of every colony
so plainly true that they need no proof
accepted only after a vote of Congress
questions.explain: The phrase presents the Declaration's principles as obvious to reasonable people, rather than as arguments to be demonstrated.

questions.q: In Notes on the State of Virginia, Jefferson printed a speech by the Mingo leader Logan that mourned:
options: the defeat of the Western Confederacy at Fallen Timbers
the death of a British officer who had been his ally
the loss of Mingo lands to the new United States
the killing of his family during the frontier violence before Dunmore's War
questions.explain: Logan's 1774 lament, recorded by others and later printed by Jefferson, became a famous speech in early American writing; some details of its background were disputed.

questions.q: Jefferson's 1790 report on weights and measures, like his coinage proposals, reflected his interest in:
options: a system based on the weight of silver alone
a system that varied by state custom
a simple decimal system based on tens
a system tied to the English royal standards
questions.explain: Jefferson favored decimal reasoning for money and measures, an idea that shaped the dollar system.

questions.q: While serving as vice president and presiding over the Senate, Jefferson wrote:
options: a bill creating the Bank of the United States
a manual of parliamentary procedure that is still influential
a treaty with France ending the Quasi-War
a plan to move the capital to Philadelphia
questions.explain: His Manual of Parliamentary Practice (1801) drew on British practice and has long influenced congressional rules.

questions.q: After hearing of Shays' Rebellion, Jefferson wrote from Paris that:
options: an occasional rebellion was not necessarily harmful to a free society
the rebels should be tried for treason at once
the Articles of Confederation were beyond repair
Massachusetts should be expelled from the union
questions.explain: Jefferson wrote that a little rebellion now and then is a good thing, a view far more relaxed than that of many Federalists.

questions.q: In which 1774 pamphlet did Jefferson write that "the God who gave us life gave us liberty at the same time"?
options: Common Sense
Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania
A Summary View of the Rights of British America
The Federalist Papers
questions.explain: The line comes from Jefferson's 1774 Summary View; a shortened version appears on a Jefferson Memorial panel that combines several of his writings.

questions.q: The political party led by Jefferson and Madison in the 1790s chose the word "Republican" to suggest that it:
options: defended republican government against what it saw as monarchical tendencies
favored a hereditary leader for the nation
opposed the Constitution's separation of powers
wanted to restore British rule in the states
questions.explain: Its members believed the Federalists leaned toward aristocracy and executive power.

questions.q: The 1785 Mount Vernon Conference, held at Washington's home, led to the Annapolis Convention because it:
options: ended a boundary war between Maryland and Virginia
settled the debt owed to British merchants
created a new federal army for the Northwest
showed that states could cooperate on shared problems like river navigation and trade
questions.explain: Maryland and Virginia commissioners discussed navigation and trade, and the success encouraged calls for a wider meeting at Annapolis in 1786.

questions.q: In his Farewell Address, Washington called religion and morality "indispensable supports" because he believed they:
options: allowed the national government to tax congregations
strengthened the habits that a republic needs from its citizens
replaced the need for written laws
gave the president power over local churches
questions.explain: Washington argued that political prosperity depended on virtue, and he linked religion and morality to public trust.

questions.q: The land on which Arlington House now stands was once part of the original federal district, but it returned to Virginia in 1846 after:
options: Congress approved retrocession of the area on the Virginia side
the Supreme Court ruled it belonged to Virginia
Maryland traded it for land near Baltimore
the capital moved to Alexandria
questions.explain: The Virginia portion, including Alexandria and what is now Arlington, was returned partly because residents felt neglected by Congress.

questions.q: The Constitution and early laws put the president in charge of the military, but they required Congress to:
options: approve each troop movement in advance
appoint every officer in the regular army
choose the commander in chief each year
declare war and provide funds for armies and navies
questions.explain: Dividing war powers reflected the framers' fear of concentrating military authority in one person.

questions.q: Lincoln often described the Declaration of Independence as a statement of:
options: a plan of government for the states
a legal code that settled the status of slavery
a principle meant to guide the nation toward greater equality
a treaty with Britain
questions.explain: Lincoln argued that the framers set a standard for liberty that later generations should work to fulfill.

questions.q: Black petitioners in Massachusetts in the 1770s, such as those seeking freedom through the courts and legislature, used which argument from the Revolution?
options: That the Constitution had already abolished slavery
That the colonists' claims to natural rights should apply to enslaved people too
That the Stamp Act had made slavery illegal
That the king had granted them freedom in 1776
questions.explain: Petitions such as those by enslaved men in 1773 and 1777 pointed to the contradiction between liberty rhetoric and slavery.

questions.q: The two-term tradition begun by Washington was later made a constitutional rule by the:
options: Twelfth Amendment
Seventeenth Amendment
Nineteenth Amendment
Twenty-second Amendment
questions.explain: The amendment, ratified in 1951, limited presidents to two elected terms after FDR's four elections.
